* [Restrict providers and models](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/restrict-providers-and-models): Scope what an access key can call
* [Configure fallback models](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/configure-fallback-models): Try another model when the first one fails
* [Observability](/docs/ai-gateway/observability): See which model served each request


# Use Hermes Agent with the AI Gateway
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/agents/hermes

Install the ngrok AI Gateway plugin for Hermes Agent to use your gateway's models as a Hermes model provider with one access key.

[Hermes Agent](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com) is Nous Research's open-source AI agent for the terminal.
The [ngrok AI Gateway plugin](https://github.com/ngrok/hermes-ngrok) adds the gateway as a Hermes model provider, so Hermes can use every model your access key reaches.

## What you'll need

* [Hermes Agent](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com) 0.21.6 or later installed.
* An [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys) from [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai/keys).

## Install the plugin

Install the plugin with the Hermes CLI:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
hermes plugins install ngrok-ai-gateway
```

Enter your access key when prompted.
Hermes saves it as `NGROK_AI_GATEWAY_KEY`.

Plugins are installed per Hermes profile, so install it again in any other profile that needs it.

## Choose a model

Run `hermes model` and select **ngrok AI Gateway**, or pass `--provider ngrok` when you start Hermes.

The model list comes from your gateway, so it shows the models your access key is allowed to call, by full catalog ID such as `openai/gpt-5.5`.
Model IDs follow the gateway's [model naming](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/models): a model ID such as `gpt-5.5`, or `provider:model` to pin a provider, such as `openai:gpt-5.5`.

## Test the connection

Send a single prompt from the command line:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
hermes chat --provider ngrok --model gpt-5.5 -q "Explain what a hash map is in two sentences."
```

Confirm the request in AI Gateway [observability](/docs/ai-gateway/observability) in [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai).

## Use a cheaper model for background tasks

Background tasks like context compression and title generation use your main model.
To send them to a cheaper model through the gateway, set the provider and model for each task in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`:

```yaml theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
auxiliary:
  compression:
    provider: ngrok
    model: gpt-5.4-mini
  title_generation:
    provider: ngrok
    model: gpt-5.4-mini
```

## What the plugin sends

The plugin sends chat and model list requests to `https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1` with your access key.
Each request carries a `User-Agent: hermes-agent/<version> (ngrok-plugin)` header.
The plugin makes no other network requests, doesn't read files, and doesn't run background processes.

* [Configure fallback models](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/configure-fallback-models): Try another model when the first one fails
* [Observability](/docs/ai-gateway/observability): See which model served each request


# Connect Coding Agents to the AI Gateway
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/agents/index

Route Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Hermes, and other coding agents through the ngrok AI Gateway to share model access and track usage.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Complete the [Quickstart](/docs/ai-gateway/quickstart) to create an access key on [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai).

Coding agents that let you change their base URL can send their model requests through the AI Gateway.
Each agent then authenticates with an ngrok.ai [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys) instead of a separate provider account, and every request shows up in one place.

Routing agents through the gateway gives you:

* One access key for every provider in the [model catalog](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/model-catalog), billed to your credits or your own provider keys
* Per-request [observability](/docs/ai-gateway/observability), with usage you can group by access key
* [Fallback models](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/configure-fallback-models) and automatic retries when a provider fails
* Limits on which providers and models each key can call
* A path to [models you run yourself](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-a-model-you-run-yourself), such as Ollama or vLLM

## Supported agents

> [card] [Claude Code](/docs/ai-gateway/agents/claude-code)
>
> Anthropic's agentic coding tool, configured with two environment variables

> [card] [Codex](/docs/ai-gateway/agents/codex)
>
> OpenAI's terminal coding agent, configured as a custom model provider

> [card] [Cursor](/docs/ai-gateway/agents/cursor)
>
> AI code editor, configured with an OpenAI base URL override

> [card] [Hermes](/docs/ai-gateway/agents/hermes)
>
> Nous Research's terminal agent, configured with the ngrok plugin

> [card] [OpenCode](/docs/ai-gateway/agents/opencode)
>
> Open-source terminal agent, configured as a custom provider

> [card] [Pi](/docs/ai-gateway/agents/pi)
>
> Terminal coding agent, configured in its models file

> [card] [Zed](/docs/ai-gateway/agents/zed)
>
> Code editor with an agent panel, configured as an OpenAI-compatible provider

> [card] [Other agents](/docs/ai-gateway/agents/other)
>
> Any agent that accepts a custom OpenAI or Anthropic base URL

## How each agent connects

Each agent speaks one API format, which decides the base URL it needs:

| Agent | API format | Base URL |
| - | - | - |
| Claude Code | Anthropic Messages | `https://gateway.ngrok.ai` |
| Codex | OpenAI Responses | `https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1` |
| Cursor | OpenAI Chat Completions | `https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1` |
| Hermes | OpenAI Chat Completions | `https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1`, set by the plugin |
| OpenCode | OpenAI Chat Completions | `https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1` |
| Pi | OpenAI Chat Completions | `https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1` |
| Zed | OpenAI Chat Completions | `https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1` |

The format also decides how an agent reaches each model.
The gateway [translates](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-any-model-with-any-sdk) each format to models that serve another one, but coding agents lean on features that the AI Gateway's automatic API format translation can't always support, such as prompt caching, reasoning, and hosted tools.
An agent works best with models that serve its own format, so Claude Code works best with Claude models and Codex with OpenAI models.

## Set up for agent traffic

Coding agents send long, streaming requests, often many per task.
A few settings keep that traffic manageable:

* Create a separate access key for each agent or teammate, so you can [group usage by access key](/docs/ai-gateway/observability) and revoke one without touching the others.
* Set `totalTimeout` to `15m` in [account settings](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/account-settings#streaming-responses).
  A saved total timeout caps the whole stream, and saving any account setting stores the `2m` default, which can cut off a long agent response.
* Scope each key to the models it needs with an [access key configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/restrict-providers-and-models).

# Use OpenCode with the AI Gateway
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/agents/opencode

Connect OpenCode to the ngrok AI Gateway to reach any model in the catalog, or a model you run yourself, with one access key.

[OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) is an open-source terminal coding agent.
It reaches the AI Gateway as a custom OpenAI-compatible provider, so one access key covers every model you add to its config.

## What you'll need

* [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai/docs/#install) installed.
* An [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys) from [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai).

## Add the gateway as a provider

Export your access key so OpenCode can read it:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
export NGROK_AI_GATEWAY_KEY="ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx"
```

Add the gateway as a provider in `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`, or in an `opencode.json` beside your project:

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "provider": {
    "ngrok": {
      "npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible",
      "name": "ngrok AI Gateway",
      "options": {
        "baseURL": "https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1",
        "apiKey": "{env:NGROK_AI_GATEWAY_KEY}"
      },
      "models": {
        "gpt-5.5": {
          "name": "GPT-5.5 (via ngrok)",
          "limit": { "context": 1050000, "output": 128000 }
        },
        "claude-sonnet-5-5": {
          "name": "Claude Sonnet 5.5 (via ngrok)",
          "limit": { "context": 1000000, "output": 128000 }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Each key in `models` is the model name OpenCode sends to the gateway.
Use any model ID from the [model catalog](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/model-catalog), or `provider:model` to pin a provider.
The `limit` values are optional, but they let OpenCode track how much context is left.

## Test the connection

Start OpenCode, run `/models`, and pick one of the models under **ngrok AI Gateway**.
Or send a single prompt from the command line:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
opencode run -m "ngrok/gpt-5.5" "Explain what a hash map is in two sentences."
```

The `-m` value is your provider ID, a slash, then the model key from `opencode.json`.

Confirm the request in AI Gateway [observability](/docs/ai-gateway/observability) in [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai).

## Use a model you run yourself

To reach a model on your own machine, register it as a [custom provider](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/custom-providers), then add its `provider:model` name to `models`, such as `ollama:llama3.2`.
See [Use a model you run yourself](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-a-model-you-run-yourself) for the full setup.

* [Observability](/docs/ai-gateway/observability): See which model served each request


# Use Other Coding Agents with the AI Gateway
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/agents/other

Connect any coding agent that accepts a custom OpenAI or Anthropic base URL to the ngrok AI Gateway with three values.

Coding agents that let you replace their built-in provider with a custom endpoint can usually reach the AI Gateway, even without a dedicated guide.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Want instructions for a specific coding agent?
> Log in to [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai), click **Give feedback**, and let the team know which one.

## What you'll need

* A coding agent that accepts a custom base URL and API key.
* An [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys) from [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai).

## Connect your agent

Every agent needs the same three values:

| Value | What to enter |
| - | - |
| Base URL | `https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1` for OpenAI-format agents, `https://gateway.ngrok.ai` for Anthropic-format agents |
| API key | Your [access key](https://app.ngrok.ai/keys), such as `ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx` |
| Model | A model ID from the [model catalog](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/model-catalog), or `provider:model` to pin a provider |

Anthropic-format agents append `/v1/messages` to the base URL themselves, so leave `/v1` off for those.

Agents that fill their model picker from `GET /v1/models` see the models your access key is allowed to call, listed by full catalog ID such as `openai/gpt-5.5`.
Those IDs work as the model value, too.
The list also includes your [virtual models](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/virtual-models), with `owned_by` set to `virtual-model`.

## Pick an API format

The gateway serves these endpoints, so an agent can use whichever format it speaks:

| Endpoint | Format |
| - | - |
| `/v1/chat/completions` | OpenAI Chat Completions |
| `/v1/responses` | OpenAI Responses |
| `/v1/messages` | Anthropic Messages |

> [!NOTE]
>
> Each endpoint also reaches models that use other API formats.
> The gateway translates the request and returns the response in the agent's format.
> See [Use any model with any SDK](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-any-model-with-any-sdk) for what translates.

Access keys work in both the `Authorization: Bearer` and `x-api-key` headers, so you don't need to match the header your agent sends.

## Test the connection

Send a prompt from the agent, then confirm the request in AI Gateway [observability](/docs/ai-gateway/observability) in [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai).
If the agent reports an error, check [Debugging](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/debugging) and the [error codes reference](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/error-codes).

## Next steps

* [Use a model you run yourself](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-a-model-you-run-yourself): Reach a model on your own machine, such as Ollama or vLLM
* [Restrict providers and models](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/restrict-providers-and-models): Scope what an access key can call


# Use the Pi Coding Agent with the AI Gateway
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/agents/pi

Connect the Pi terminal coding agent to the ngrok AI Gateway to reach any model in the catalog, or a model you run yourself.

[Pi](https://pi.dev) is a terminal coding agent.
It reaches the AI Gateway as a custom provider in its models file, so one access key covers every model you list there.

## What you'll need

* [Pi](https://pi.dev) installed.
* An [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys) from [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai).

## Add the gateway as a provider

Export your access key so Pi can read it:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
export NGROK_AI_GATEWAY_KEY="ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx"
```

Add the gateway as a provider in `~/.pi/agent/models.json`:

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "providers": {
    "ngrok": {
      "baseUrl": "https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1",
      "apiKey": "$NGROK_AI_GATEWAY_KEY",
      "api": "openai-completions",
      "models": [
        { "id": "gpt-5.5" },
        { "id": "claude-sonnet-5-5" }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

`id` is the model name Pi sends to the gateway: a model ID from the [model catalog](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/model-catalog), or `provider:model` to pin a provider.
It's the only field a model entry needs, though you can add `name`, `contextWindow`, and `maxTokens` to label it and track context accurately.

## Test the connection

Send a single prompt from the command line:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
pi --provider ngrok --model "gpt-5.5" -p "Explain what a hash map is in two sentences."
```

In an interactive session, run `/model` and pick one of the **ngrok** models instead.

Confirm the request in AI Gateway [observability](/docs/ai-gateway/observability) in [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai).

## Use a model you run yourself

To reach a model on your own machine, register it as a [custom provider](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/custom-providers), then add its `provider:model` name to `models`, such as `ollama:llama3.2`.
See [Use a model you run yourself](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-a-model-you-run-yourself) for the full setup.

* [Restrict providers and models](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/restrict-providers-and-models): Scope what an access key can call
* [Configure fallback models](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/configure-fallback-models): Try another model when the first one fails
* [Observability](/docs/ai-gateway/observability): See which model served each request


# Use Zed with the AI Gateway
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/agents/zed

Connect the Zed editor's agent panel to the ngrok AI Gateway as an OpenAI-compatible provider to use catalog or self-hosted models.

[Zed](https://zed.dev) is a code editor with a built-in agent panel.
It reaches the AI Gateway as an OpenAI-compatible LLM provider, so the agent panel can use any model you list in your settings.

## What you'll need

* [Zed](https://zed.dev/download) installed.
* An [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys) from [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai).

## Add the gateway as a provider

Add the provider to your Zed `settings.json`:

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "language_models": {
    "openai_compatible": {
      "ngrok": {
        "api_url": "https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1",
        "available_models": [
          {
            "name": "gpt-5.5",
            "display_name": "GPT-5.5 (via ngrok)",
            "max_tokens": 1050000
          },
```

For each model:

# AI Gateway API
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/overview

Set up and run your AI Gateway from your own code with the management API.

***

The ngrok.ai API lets you manage ngrok.ai directly from your code, so you don't have to rely on the dashboard.

You can use it to create access keys, add provider keys, set up routing and access rules, register custom providers, check usage, and keep an eye on your credit balance.

The API doesn't handle model requests itself.
To call models, send your requests to `https://gateway.ngrok.ai` using an access key.

## Base URL

When you make requests to the ngrok.ai API, send them to:

```text theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
https://api.ngrok.ai
```

The ngrok.ai API uses JSON for both requests and responses, and you must make all calls over HTTPS.

## Authentication

To authenticate, include your [ngrok.ai API key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys#credentials-overview) in the `Authorization` header of each request:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
curl https://api.ngrok.ai/access-keys \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY"
```

You can create and manage your ngrok.ai API key on the settings page in the dashboard.
Treat this key like a secret, since it allows you to manage the resources in your account.

## Scopes

Each route needs a scope.
An API key can call a route only when it has that scope.
The two key types accept different scopes when you create them:

* **Access keys** accept `ai-gateway:inference:request` for inference requests.
* **API keys** accept one or more AI Gateway management scopes, such as `ai-gateway:access-keys:read`, which lets the key list and view access keys and access key configurations.
  Read-only management scopes count.

Most resources have a `read` scope, to view them, and a `write` scope, to create, change, and delete them.

| Resource | Scopes | What it covers |
| - | - | - |
| Access keys | `ai-gateway:access-keys:read`, `ai-gateway:access-keys:write` | Access keys and access key configurations. |
| API keys | `ai-gateway:api-keys:read`, `ai-gateway:api-keys:write` | ngrok.ai API keys. |
| Credits | `ai-gateway:credits:read`, `ai-gateway:credits:write` | The credit balance, transactions, and purchases. |
| Providers | `ai-gateway:providers:read`, `ai-gateway:providers:write` | Providers, provider keys, and the model list. |
| Settings | `ai-gateway:settings:read`, `ai-gateway:settings:write` | Gateway configuration and firewall policies. |
| Usage | `ai-gateway:usage:read` | Usage data and request logs. |
| Virtual models | `ai-gateway:virtual-models:read`, `ai-gateway:virtual-models:write` | Virtual models. |

Access keys use `ai-gateway:inference:request` for model requests to `https://gateway.ngrok.ai`.
This scope doesn't grant access to the management API.

### Missing scopes

When an API key calls a route without the scope it needs, the API returns `403 Forbidden` and names the missing scope:

```text theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
You don't have permission to perform this action. Your credentials are missing the 'ai-gateway:access-keys:write' scope.
```

To fix the error, add the scope to the API key.

## OpenAPI spec

A public OpenAPI 3.0 spec describes the API.
Use it to generate a client in any language, or load it into your API tooling:

```text theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
https://api.ngrok.ai/openapi.yaml
```

## What you can manage

Use the AI Gateway API to manage:

* [Access keys](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/access-keys/list): Manage keys for making gateway requests
* [Access key configurations](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/access-key-configurations/list): Manage access controls and rules for which providers, models, and keys an access key can use
* [Providers](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/providers/list): Manage which providers the gateway can route to
* [Provider keys](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/provider-keys/list): Manage your credentials for providers
* [API keys](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/api-keys/list): Manage keys that grant ngrok.ai API access
* [Configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/gateway-config/get): Manage your account level gateway settings
* [Credits](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/credits/balance): View your credit balance and transactions, and start a purchase
* [Models](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/models/list): List every model your account can reach, with pricing and provider metrics
* [Virtual models](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/virtual-models/list): Manage names that stand for an ordered list of models to try in turn
* [Usage](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/usage/list): View data on requests, tokens, providers, models, and costs

## Common workflows

Use the ngrok.ai API to automate common setup and operational tasks.

### Create access keys

Create access keys for applications, environments, teams, or customers.
Each access key can have its own configuration for routing, model access, and provider credentials.

### Add provider keys

Store upstream provider credentials so ngrok.ai can call providers on your behalf without exposing those credentials in your application code.

Define access key configurations to control which providers and models an access key can call, and which provider keys are used for upstream authentication.

### Register custom providers

Create custom providers for self-hosted models, private deployments, or other OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible APIs.

### Monitor usage and credits

Query usage and credit data to track requests, tokens, costs, and remaining balance.

# Access Keys
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys

Learn how AI Gateway access keys differ from provider keys and how to create, rotate, and revoke them in the dashboard or API.

An **access key** authenticates your application to `https://gateway.ngrok.ai`.
Send it with every request—the gateway uses it to verify who is calling and whether the request is allowed through.

## Access keys vs provider keys

The AI Gateway splits authentication into two credentials so your application never handles upstream secrets.

| | Access key | Provider key |
| - | - | - |
| **What it is** | The credential your app sends to the gateway | An upstream API key for OpenAI, Anthropic, or another provider |
| **Where it lives** | In your application | In [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai), attached through an [access key configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations) |
| **Who uses it** | Your code, as the SDK's `api_key` | The AI Gateway, injected server-side on each request |

Because the two are separate, you can rotate or revoke an access key for one client without touching your [provider keys](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/attaching-provider-keys), and your upstream secrets never ship in client code.

Many built-in providers, including **OpenAI**, **Anthropic**, **Google**, and **DeepSeek**, let you [pay with credits](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/pay-with-credits).
There are no provider keys to store at all.

See [How It Works](/docs/ai-gateway/how-it-works) for the full request flow.

## Use in your application

```python theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1",
    api_key="ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx"  # Your access key
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]
)
```

See the [Quickstart](/docs/ai-gateway/quickstart) to create your first key.

## Create and manage keys

Create a separate key per application or team so you can revoke one client without affecting others.

### Via the ngrok dashboard

1. Open [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai) → **Keys**.
2. Click **New access key**.
3. Enter a description, choose what the key can call, and optionally set an expiration and assign a configuration.
4. Copy the token immediately—it's only shown once.

### Via the AI Gateway API

1. Create an [AI Gateway API key](#credentials-overview) with the `ai-gateway:access-keys:write` [scope](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/overview#scopes).
2. Send a request to the [Access Keys API](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/access-keys/create), authorized with that key:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
curl -X POST https://api.ngrok.ai/access-keys \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "description": "Production web app", "scopes": ["ai-gateway:inference:request"] }'
```

## Things to know

### Scopes decide what a key can call

An access key needs the `ai-gateway:inference:request` scope to send model requests.
Access key creation doesn't accept management scopes or scopes for other ngrok products.
The gateway rejects a request that the key's scopes don't allow.

### Keys can expire

When you create a key, you can set an expiration time.
After that time, the gateway rejects the key.
A key without an expiration time stays valid until you delete it.

### Your key token is only shown once

When you create a key, the token (starting with `ngrok_pat_`) is displayed exactly once.
If you lose it, delete the key and create a new one.

### Requests require credits

Every request consumes [credits](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/credits) for the ngrok.ai processing fee.
When you pay with credits, credits also cover model cost.
When you bring your own key, model costs go to your provider account.

When your balance reaches zero, new requests fail until you purchase more credits.

### Invalid keys are rejected

The gateway immediately rejects malformed or deleted access keys with a `401 Unauthorized`.
See [Error Codes](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/error-codes) to look up that and other gateway responses.

## Credentials overview

| Credential | What it's for |
| - | - |
| **ngrok.ai access keys** | Authenticate AI requests to `gateway.ngrok.ai` (required) |
| **ngrok.ai API keys** | Automate AI Gateway resources via `api.ngrok.ai` |
| **ngrok API keys** | Manage ngrok platform resources via the [ngrok API](https://api.ngrok.com) |
| **Your provider keys** | Upstream credentials. See [Bring your own provider key](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/attaching-provider-keys) |

# Bring Your Own Keys
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/bring-your-own-keys

Decide when to use your own provider API keys with ngrok.ai instead of paying with credits, then set them up for built-in or custom providers.

Bringing your own keys is necessary when:

* you want upstream billing on your provider account
* you need a built-in provider you [can't pay for with credits](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/model-catalog#billing-and-provider-credentials)
* you're running [custom providers](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/custom-providers)

Your application authenticates with an [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys). Store provider keys in [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai) and attach them through an [access key configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations).

## Built-in providers

| | Providers you can pay for with credits | Other built-in providers |
| - | - | - |
| Provider account needed | Optional | Yes |
| Default credentials | ngrok.ai supplies the key, paid with credits | Provider key required in configuration |
| What credits pay for | Processing fee; plus model cost when you pay with credits | Processing fee only |

For providers you can pay for with credits, create a configuration routing rule with **Bring your own API key** instead of **ngrok** when you want to use your provider account.

## Custom providers

Custom providers are endpoints you define, such as Ollama, vLLM, or any OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible API. See [Use a model you run yourself](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-a-model-you-run-yourself).

Custom providers require provider keys in the configuration when the upstream needs authentication. See [Custom providers](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/custom-providers).

## Setup flow

1. [Add provider keys](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/attaching-provider-keys#add-a-provider-key).
2. Create an [access key configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations) with routing rules and scope.
3. Assign the configuration to an [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys).
4. Send requests with the access key only.

# AI Gateway Credits
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/credits

Buy ngrok.ai credits, turn on automatic top-ups, and see how requests consume credits and what happens to them when you run out.

AI Gateway credits are a prepaid balance you buy in [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai).
Every request through `https://gateway.ngrok.ai` pays a small [processing fee](#processing-fee) from your credits.
If you don't use your own provider key, credits also pay for the model.
See [How credits are consumed](#how-credits-are-consumed).

## Accounts and plans

You don't need an ngrok subscription to use the AI Gateway.
Sign in to [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai) with your ngrok account, buy credits, and create an [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys).

AI Gateway credits are separate from your ngrok plan.
Your ngrok plan doesn't pay for AI Gateway usage, and credits don't pay for other ngrok features.

| Manage | Where |
| - | - |
| Access keys, providers, credits, and usage | [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai) |
| Your ngrok plan, team members, tunnels, and endpoints | [dashboard.ngrok.com](https://dashboard.ngrok.com) |

To reach a model you run yourself through an [internal endpoint](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/custom-providers), set up the endpoint in dashboard.ngrok.com.
Some ngrok features need a paid plan; see [pricing](https://ngrok.com/pricing).

## Purchasing credits

1. Open the [Billing page](https://app.ngrok.ai/billing) and select **Add credits**.
   If you haven't saved a card yet, you'll add one first.
2. Pick an amount, or enter your own.
   The minimum is \$5, and your balance can be at most \$500.
3. Select **Buy** to confirm.

To buy credits from code, use the [Credits API](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/credits/purchase-create).

Credits expire **one year** after purchase.

## Automatic top-up

Automatic top-up adds credits from your saved card when your balance runs low.

To set it up:

1. Open the [Billing page](https://app.ngrok.ai/billing) and make sure you have a saved card.
2. Select **Enable auto top-up**, then turn on **Enable auto top-up** in the dialog.
3. Set **When your balance reaches** (at least \$5) and **Top up to** (up to \$500).
4. Optional: select **Set a spending limit** and enter a **Maximum spend every billing period**.
5. Select **Save changes**.

## How credits are consumed

| If the request uses | Credits pay for | You pay separately |
| - | - | - |
| An ngrok.ai key | Processing fee and model usage, including [hosted tools](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/hosted-tools) like web search | Nothing |
| Your own provider key | Processing fee | Model usage, billed by your provider |
| A model you run yourself | Processing fee | Your own infrastructure |

## Balance tracking

You can view your balance on the [Billing page](https://app.ngrok.ai/billing), or via the API:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
curl https://api.ngrok.ai/credits/balance \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY"
```

## What happens when credits run out

When your credit balance reaches zero, the gateway rejects new requests with HTTP 402 and [`ERR_NGROK_27206`](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/error-codes#err_ngrok_27206) until you purchase more credits.
That's true even if you use your own provider keys, since every request pays a small processing fee from your credits.

app.ngrok.ai warns you before that happens.
Your balance shows next to **Credits** in the sidebar, and the [Billing page](https://app.ngrok.ai/billing) shows a warning when it drops below \$20, again below \$5, and when it reaches \$0.
Once the balance reaches \$0, **Overview** shows **Add credits**, and the [playground](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/playground#if-your-balance-runs-out) is covered by a **Purchase credits** form until you buy more.

To avoid this, turn on [automatic top-up](#automatic-top-up) so your balance refills before it runs out.

The balance updates shortly after usage, so requests already in flight can take it slightly below zero.
The [balance API](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/credits/balance) reports a negative value when that happens.

## Processing fee

Every successful request through the gateway incurs a processing fee at **USD \$0.05 per million tokens**.
The fee is based on the tokens in your request and response.
It applies to all traffic—requests paid with credits, your own [provider keys](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/attaching-provider-keys), and [custom providers](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/custom-providers)—and doesn't vary by model or provider.
With [`ngrok/auto`](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/automatic-model-selection#billing), the tokens ngrok.ai reads to pick a model also count toward the fee.

When you pay with credits, credits also cover the provider's model cost.
When you bring your own key, model costs stay on your provider account and credits cover only the processing fee.

# Custom Providers
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/custom-providers

Decide when to connect your own model server to ngrok.ai as a custom provider, and check which kinds of URLs the gateway can reach.

**Custom providers** are upstream endpoints you define, such as self-hosted Ollama or vLLM, a private deployment, or any OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible API not in the [built-in catalog](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/model-catalog).

Use a custom provider when you want the AI Gateway to call a model running on your machine, private network, or cloud GPU.

Traffic still authenticates to the gateway with an [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys).
Attach provider keys and routing rules through an [access key configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations).

## When to use one

Use a custom provider when:

* You run models locally with Ollama, LM Studio, or vLLM.
* You host models on your own cloud infrastructure.
* You have a private OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible API.
* You need a provider that isn't in the built-in catalog.

## What a custom provider defines

A custom provider tells the gateway:

* Which provider ID to use in requests, such as `my-ollama`.
* Which base URL to call, such as `https://my-ollama.internal`.
* Which API surface the endpoint supports.
* Which model IDs are available.

A model ID can't match the name of one of your [virtual models](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/virtual-models), without regard to case.

You call custom provider models with the same `provider:model` format as built-in providers:

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "model": "my-ollama:llama3.2",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
}
```

## URL requirements

| URL type | Scheme | Example |
| - | - | - |
| External | `https://` only | `https://api.example.com/v1` |
| ngrok internal | `http://` or `https://` | `https://my-service.internal` |

HTTP is only allowed for ngrok `.internal` endpoints.
External URLs must use HTTPS.

## Self-hosted on a local network

To reach models on your machine or private network, expose the service with an ngrok internal endpoint, then use that URL as the custom provider's `baseUrl`.
Reaching internal endpoints may require an ngrok platform plan.
See [Credits](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/credits).

For the full setup flow, see [Use a model you run yourself](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-a-model-you-run-yourself).

# AI Gateway Firewall
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/firewall

Check what your agents send to a model and block risky tool calls before your agent runs them, with rules you attach to access keys.

Agents run tools with real access to your machines, repos, and secrets, and one bad tool call can do lasting damage.
An agent can delete an operating system by accident with a single shell command, push to a public repo whose name is close to your private one, or send your company's secrets and API keys somewhere they don't belong.

Firewall stops those calls in the AI Gateway, before your agent runs them:

* **No code changes**: you attach a policy to [access keys](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys), so every agent that uses those keys gets the same checks.
* **Blocked before it runs**: Firewall checks each tool call the model returns before your agent receives it, even in a streamed response.
* **Agents recover**: a block returns a normal response that tells the model what was blocked and why, so the agent can change course instead of failing.

You describe what to check in a **Firewall policy**: a named set of rules, a mode, and what to do when a check can't run.

To set one up, see [Guard agent tool calls with Firewall](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/firewall-policies).

> [!NOTE]
>
> Firewall is an early release.
> Some behavior on this page may change as the feature develops.

## Where checks run

```mermaid theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
sequenceDiagram
  participant Agent
  participant Gateway as gateway.ngrok.ai
  participant Model as Provider
  Agent->>Gateway: Request (messages, tool results, tool definitions)
  Note over Gateway: Request rules
  Gateway->>Model: Request, if no rule blocks it
  Model->>Gateway: Response with tool calls
  Note over Gateway: Response rules
  Gateway->>Agent: Response, with blocked tool calls held back
```

Each rule runs at one of two points:

* **Request rules** run before the gateway sends the request to the model.
  They read the conversation, the results of tools the agent ran, and the tools the agent offers the model.
  A blocked request never reaches the model.
* **Response rules** run on each tool call the model returns.
  A blocked tool call is removed from the response, so your agent never receives it and can't run it.

Firewall checks [OpenAI Chat Completions](/docs/ai-gateway/sdks/openai) (`/v1/chat/completions`), [OpenAI Responses](/docs/ai-gateway/sdks/openai#supported-endpoints) (`/v1/responses`), [Anthropic Messages](/docs/ai-gateway/sdks/anthropic) (`/v1/messages`), and [Gemini generate content](/docs/ai-gateway/sdks/google#generate-content-requests) (`generateContent` and `streamGenerateContent`) requests, both streamed and not streamed.
That covers agents that call those endpoints through the gateway, such as [Claude Code](/docs/ai-gateway/agents/claude-code) and [Codex](/docs/ai-gateway/agents/codex).
For other endpoints, see [Things to know](#things-to-know).

## Rules

Each rule has a type, which says how it matches, and a tier, which says what happens when it matches.

### Rule types

| Type | How it matches | Model call |
| - | - | - |
| **Tool names** | Matches tool names exactly, with `*` as a wildcard. For example, `mcp__github__*` matches every tool from a GitHub MCP server. | No |
| **Regex** | Matches an [RE2](https://github.com/google/re2/wiki/Syntax) pattern against the text. For a tool call, the text is the tool name, a space, and the arguments. | No |
| **Decision** | A decision model judges the text against a rule you write in plain language, such as "Deletes files outside the project directory." The rule matches when the model's confidence reaches the rule's threshold. | Yes |

Tool names and regex rules are fast and predictable.
Use a decision rule when the risk depends on intent or context that a pattern can't capture.

Decision rules use [Jev](/docs/ai-gateway/providers/typesafeai), a decision model.
Jev is a separate model that ngrok calls to judge the rule, not the model your request asks for.

### What a rule reads

| Part | Checked | What it contains |
| - | - | - |
| **Messages** | Before the model | System, developer, user, and assistant turns, including earlier tool calls. |
| **Tool results** | Before the model | The output of tools your agent ran, such as file contents or web pages. |
| **Tool definitions** | Before the model | The tools the request offers the model: names, descriptions, and parameters. |
| **Tool calls** | After the model | Each tool call the model returns. |

A rule reads either request parts or tool calls, not both.
Tool names rules read tool definitions or tool calls.

Decision rules on request parts read the system and developer messages plus the newest input: the latest user message and any tool results it carries.
Regex rules on request parts read the whole conversation.

### Tiers

| Tier | What happens when the rule matches |
| - | - |
| **Hard block** | Always blocks. |
| **Soft block** | Blocks, unless an **Allow** rule in the same policy also matches at the same point. |
| **Allow** | Never blocks. It lets through something a soft block rule in the same policy would block. |

Use soft block and allow together for exceptions.
For example, a soft block regex rule that matches `git push` and an allow regex rule that matches `git push origin feature/` block every push except pushes to feature branches.

## Mode and errors

A policy's **mode** decides whether matches block anything:

* **Enforce** blocks requests and tool calls that match a blocking rule.
* **Dry run** checks everything and reports what matched, but lets it all through.
  Use it to test a policy on real traffic before you enforce it.

A check can fail to run, for example when the decision model times out.
**On error** decides what happens then:

* **Block** treats what it couldn't check as blocked.
  This only applies in Enforce mode.
* **Continue** lets it through and reports that it wasn't checked.

If Firewall can't read the tool calls in a response at all, and the policy uses Enforce and Block, the request fails with a `500` error instead.

## Where a policy applies

| Scope | Applies to | Where you set it |
| - | - | - |
| **All access keys** | Every key in your account, including keys you create later. This policy is your **baseline**. | The policy's **Apply to** setting, or `firewallPolicyId` in the [gateway configuration API](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/gateway-config/update). |
| **Access key configurations** | Only keys that use a configuration that picks the policy. | The policy's **Apply to** setting, the **Firewall** section of an [access key configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations), or `firewallPolicyId` in the [configurations API](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/access-key-configurations/update). |
| **One request** | A single request. | The [`plugins` field](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/firewall#the-plugins-field) of the request body. |

An account has at most one baseline, and a configuration picks at most one policy.

### How policies combine

A request can be checked by up to three policies: the baseline, the policy of its key's configuration, and a policy in the request.
Firewall runs every rule from all of them, so a policy can add checks but never remove one:

* Each policy keeps its own **Mode** and **On error** setting.
  A Dry run policy only reports, even when your baseline enforces, so you can try a new policy on keys that already have one.
* An allow rule only overrides soft block rules in its own policy.
  A request can't allow what your baseline blocks.

When you make a policy your baseline, configurations that picked the same policy stop picking it, so its rules don't run twice.

## What your agent sees

A block is not an HTTP error.
The gateway returns a normal `200` response, so your agent keeps working and the model can react to the block:

* **Blocked request**: the response holds one assistant message that says which rule blocked the request.
* **Blocked tool call**: the gateway replaces the call with assistant text that names the tool and the rule, and tells the model not to retry it with the same arguments.

The response also carries a `safeguard_results` field, and the `Ngrok-AIG-Firewall-Request` header reports request rule results.
See [What a blocked caller gets](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/firewall#what-a-blocked-caller-gets) for the exact formats.

## Things to know

* **Other endpoints**: Firewall can't check requests to other endpoints, such as the [Gemini Interactions API](/docs/ai-gateway/sdks/google#supported-endpoints).
  **On error** decides what happens to them.
  If a policy that applies to the key uses Enforce and Block, the gateway rejects them with [`ERR_NGROK_27228`](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/error-codes#err_ngrok_27228).
  Otherwise, they go through unchecked with the header `Ngrok-AIG-Firewall: unscreened; reason=unsupported_endpoint`.
* **Legacy functions**: Firewall checks tool calls, not the function calls a model returns for the legacy Chat Completions `functions` field.
  When a policy has response rules, **On error** decides those requests the same way, and the header reason is `legacy_functions`.
  Send `tools` instead of `functions`.
* **Streamed Gemini function call arguments**: with `streamFunctionCallArguments`, Gemini sends each function call in fragments, which Firewall doesn't join.
  When a policy has response rules, **On error** decides those requests the same way, and the header reason is `stream_function_call_arguments`.
  When they go through, request rules still run, but tool calls aren't checked.
* **OpenAI-defined tools**: in a Responses request, Firewall can't read the arguments of tools that OpenAI defines and your app runs, such as local shell, computer use, and `apply_patch`.
  Tool names rules still match these calls by name, such as `local_shell` or `apply_patch`.
  For other rules, **On error** decides.
* **Provider-run tools**: tools that the provider runs before the response returns, such as OpenAI and Anthropic web search or Gemini code execution, never reach your agent, so Firewall doesn't check them.
* **`previous_response_id`**: when Firewall blocks a tool call in a Responses request, OpenAI still keeps the original call.
  If your next request uses `previous_response_id`, OpenAI expects a tool output for a call your app never received.
  Send the conversation in `input` instead.
* **Latency**: tool names and regex rules add almost no latency.
  Each decision rule calls the decision model, which can add up to 1.5 seconds before the check counts as failed.
* **Streaming**: in Enforce mode, the gateway holds each streamed tool call until its checks finish, so your agent never receives a call that wasn't checked.
  The rest of the stream keeps flowing.
* **Usage logs**: for now, Firewall results don't appear in [usage logs](/docs/ai-gateway/observability).
  Read the response headers and `safeguard_results` to see what Firewall did.

# Hosted Tool Billing
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/hosted-tools

Hosted tools bill in units like search calls or generated images, and some also add tokens. You can read each tool's rate from the List Models API.

Some providers run tools for the model on their own servers, such as web search, code execution, and image generation.
When you [pay with credits](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/pay-with-credits), credits pay for these hosted tools at the provider's price, on top of the model's token cost.
When you [bring your own provider key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/bring-your-own-keys), your provider bills the tool directly.

## Supported tools

The gateway prices these hosted tools when the provider and model offer them:

* `web_search`, `web_fetch`, `url_context`, `image_search`, and `x_search`
* `code_execution` and `code_interpreter`
* `file_search`
* `image_generation`
* `maps`

Not every model supports every tool.
Each provider's price list sets which tools a model offers and what they cost.

## How hosted tools are billed

Credits pay for a hosted tool in the unit the provider bills, such as a search call, a generated image, or an hour of container time.
Some tools also bill tokens, such as the search results a model reads or the tokens an image model uses.

Some tools cost nothing beyond the model's tokens.
Those tools have no separate rate, and their usage bills at the model's token rates.

The tokens a hosted tool adds to the prompt also count toward the [processing fee](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/credits#processing-fee).

When the gateway [translates a request](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-any-model-with-any-sdk#hosted-tools) for a model that uses another API format, the tool bills at the rate of the tool the provider ran.

Free allowances a provider grants, such as free container hours, don't reduce what credits pay.
Credits pay for every hosted-tool call at the listed rate.

## Find a tool's price

The [List Models API](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/models/list) returns each tool's rates in `providers[].pricing.rates`, next to the model's token rates.
A hosted-tool rate has the tool name as its `type`.

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
curl https://api.ngrok.ai/v1/models \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY"
```

For example, OpenAI's `gpt-4o` lists two web search rates:

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "currency": "USD",
  "rates": [
    { "type": "prompt", "unit": "token", "price": "0.0000025" },
    { "type": "web_search", "unit": "request", "price": "0.01" },
    {
      "type": "web_search",
      "unit": "request",
      "price": "0.025",
      "conditions": {
        "tool_version": "web_search_preview",
        "model_reasoning": false,
        "content_tokens": "free"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

Each rate is a price in `currency` per `unit`.
Common hosted-tool units are `request`, `image`, `hour`, `gb_day`, `query`, `grounded_prompt`, and `container_session`.

When a tool has more than one rate, `conditions` says which requests each rate applies to:

| Condition | Meaning |
| - | - |
| `tool_version` | The tool version this rate applies to. |
| `model_reasoning` | Whether this rate applies to a reasoning model. |
| `with_tool_at_least` | Another tool, at this dated version or later, whose presence selects this rate. |
| `content_tokens` | Whether the content the tool returns bills as tokens or is free. |
| `model` | The second model whose tokens this rate prices, such as the image model behind `image_generation`. |
| `tier` | The size this rate applies to, such as a container memory class. |
| `minimum_billable` | The smallest billable quantity, such as `5m` for a container. |
| `session_minutes` | The length of one billed session block. A partial block bills as a whole block. |

A tool that bills only through the model's tokens has no rate of its own in the list.

## Limits and availability

If a model's price list doesn't include a hosted tool, you can't pay for that tool with credits on that model.
The gateway rejects the request with [`ERR_NGROK_27238`](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/error-codes#err_ngrok_27238) before it reaches the provider.
To use the tool, remove it from the request, pick another model, or [attach your own provider key](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/attaching-provider-keys).

[Custom providers](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/custom-providers) don't use hosted-tool rates, because you set their pricing yourself.

# AI Gateway Models
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/models

Choose and name the models in your ngrok AI Gateway requests, and list fallback models for the gateway to try next.

Models are the AI systems that process your requests.
You specify the model in each request body, and you can use an [access key configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations) to restrict which models an access key may call.

## Specifying models

### Model name only

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "model": "gpt-4o",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
}
```

The gateway looks up `gpt-4o` in the [model catalog](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/model-catalog) and routes to OpenAI.
If OpenAI fails, it can try other providers that serve the same model.

The full catalog ID, `author/model` such as `openai/gpt-4o`, works the same way.

### Provider prefix

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "model": "anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
}
```

Use `provider:model` when you want to force a specific provider or target [a model you run yourself](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-a-model-you-run-yourself).

## Multiple models (failover)

List fallback models with the `models` array:

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "model": "gpt-4o",
  "models": ["gpt-4o-mini", "anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6"],
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
}
```

The gateway tries `model` first, then each entry in `models` in order, until one succeeds.

## Virtual models

A virtual model is a name you save in your account, such as `chat-default`, that stands for an ordered list of models.
Send the name as `model`, and the gateway tries the models in order:

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "model": "chat-default",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
}
```

Use one to change the models your apps use from the gateway, without changing their code or requests.
It also gives failover to a client that can't send a `models` array.
See [Virtual models](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/virtual-models).

## Unknown models (pass-through)

If a model isn't in the catalog, the gateway still routes it when you include a provider prefix:

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "model": "openai:some-new-model",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
}
```

The provider returns an error if the model doesn't exist.
The access key's configuration must still allow pass-through models.

## Model and provider names

Model names aren't case-sensitive: `gpt-4o`, `GPT-4o`, and `Gpt-4O` all resolve to the same model.
The gateway matches provider names exactly, so use the lowercase **Provider ID** from the [model catalog](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/model-catalog).

Name models and providers by their primary catalog ID.
The gateway doesn't resolve alternate names for either.

## Model capabilities

Models differ in input/output modalities, context window, and features.
See the [model catalog](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/model-catalog) for details.

# Open-Weight Models
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/open-weight-models

Learn what open-weight means, how open-weight models behave in the ngrok AI Gateway, and which models in the catalog are open-weight.

An open-weight model is one whose author publishes the trained weights for anyone to download.
You can call it through a hosted provider, like any other model, or run the same weights on your own hardware.

## What open-weight means

The weights are the parameters a model learns during training.
With a closed model, such as GPT-5.5 or Claude, only the author and its partners can run the weights, so you can only reach the model through their APIs.
With an open-weight model, the author releases the weights under a license, and any provider or person can serve them.

Open-weight isn't the same as open source.
Authors often publish the weights without the training data or training code.
Licenses also differ: some, like Apache 2.0 and MIT, allow almost any use, while others, like the Llama Community License, add conditions.
Check the license on the author's model card before you use a model commercially or fine-tune it.

## What it means in the AI Gateway

You send requests to open-weight models the same way you send them to closed models.
Being open-weight changes where the model can run:

* **More than one provider can serve it.**
  When several providers in the [model catalog](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/model-catalog) serve the same model, the gateway can [fail over](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/configure-fallback-models) between them.
  Use a `provider:model` prefix to keep requests on one provider.
* **You can run it yourself.**
  Serve the weights with a tool like Ollama or vLLM, then [add it as a custom provider](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-a-model-you-run-yourself).
  Your apps call it through the same gateway endpoint and access keys as your hosted models.
* **You can mix self-hosted and hosted copies.**
  List your own server first and a hosted provider as a fallback, so requests keep working when your server is down.

For example, this request tries GPT-OSS 20B on your own Ollama server first, then on Groq:

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "model": "ollama:gpt-oss:20b",
  "models": ["groq:openai/gpt-oss-20b"],
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
}
```

# AI Gateway Providers
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/providers

Learn the difference between built-in and custom providers in the ngrok AI Gateway and how the gateway picks a provider for each request.

Providers are the AI services that host and serve models.
The AI Gateway routes your requests to providers and handles authentication, failover, and observability.

Manage providers at [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai).
If you're deciding which setup path to use, start with [Choose how to reach providers](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/configuring-providers).
The dashboard separates **built-in** catalog providers from **custom** providers you define.

## Built-in providers

Built-in providers are public AI APIs with a known model catalog: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Groq, and others listed in the [model catalog](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/model-catalog).
You can send requests with an [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys).
Your access key authenticates you to the gateway, not to the upstream provider.

For many built-in providers, including **OpenAI**, **Anthropic**, **Google**, and **DeepSeek**, the AI Gateway can supply the provider credentials when you have [credits](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/credits).
The [model catalog](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/model-catalog#billing-and-provider-credentials) shows which providers support it.
You aren't required to have your own provider account or provider API keys—the AI Gateway handles upstream authentication and bills model cost through credits.

For providers you can't pay for with credits, [bring your own provider key](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/attaching-provider-keys#add-a-provider-key).
Model costs go to your provider account; credits still cover the gateway processing fee.
This is generally referred to as BYOK (bring your own key).

## Custom providers

Custom providers are upstream endpoints you define, such as self-hosted Ollama or vLLM, a private deployment, or any OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible API that isn't in the built-in catalog.
See [Use a model you run yourself](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-a-model-you-run-yourself).

Custom providers require a provider key when the upstream needs authentication.
See [Custom providers](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/custom-providers) for the concept.

>

>
> Desktop app for local model inference.

> [card] [Azure OpenAI](/docs/ai-gateway/custom-providers/azure-openai)
>
> Microsoft's OpenAI service on Azure.

## How provider selection works

When a request arrives, the gateway determines which provider to use:

1. **Explicit provider prefix**: if the model name includes a provider prefix (for example, `openai:gpt-4o` or `openrouter:anthropic/claude-3.5-sonnet`), the gateway uses that provider
2. **Catalog lookup**: the gateway looks up the model ID in its [catalog](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/model-catalog) to find the default provider
3. **Request selection**: [model names](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/model-selection-strategies) and fallback lists can override the default

# Connect Azure OpenAI to the AI Gateway
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/custom-providers/azure-openai

Connect an Azure OpenAI deployment to the ngrok AI Gateway as a custom provider, including multiple deployments and regions.

[Azure OpenAI Service](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/ai-services/openai-service) provides OpenAI models on Microsoft Azure.
Connect your deployment to the AI Gateway as a [custom provider](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/custom-providers).

## What you'll need

* [ngrok account](https://app.ngrok.ai) with AI Gateway access
* [Azure OpenAI Service](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/ai-services/openai-service) resource with a deployed model
* An [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys) from [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai)

## Overview

Azure OpenAI uses deployment-specific URLs and requires an `api-version` query parameter.
The gateway injects your Azure API key server-side.

```mermaid theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
graph LR
    A[Client] --> B[gateway.ngrok.ai]
    B --> C[Azure OpenAI]
```

## Getting started

### 1. Gather Azure details

From the Azure Portal, collect:

1. **Resource endpoint**: `https://your-resource.openai.azure.com`
2. **API key**: from **Keys and Endpoint**
3. **Deployment name**: the name of your model deployment
4. **API version**: a supported version (for example `2024-02-15-preview`)

### 2. Create the custom provider

Azure requires the deployment path and `api-version` in the base URL.
See [Create a custom provider](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-a-model-you-run-yourself#create-a-custom-provider) with:

* **Provider ID**: `azure-openai`
* **Base URL**: `https://your-resource.openai.azure.com/openai/deployments/your-deployment?api-version=2024-02-15-preview`
* **API format**: OpenAI Chat Completions
* **Models**: the model name for this deployment (for example `gpt-4o`)

> [!NOTE]
>
> Include `api-version` as a query parameter on the base URL.
> Azure rejects requests without it.

### 3. Store your Azure API key

[Add a provider key](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/attaching-provider-keys#add-a-provider-key) for your Azure deployment.

### 4. Configure access

Create an [access key configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations) that:

1. Allows the `azure-openai` provider in the access scope
2. Adds a routing rule for `azure-openai` with **Bring your own API key** and your stored key attached

Assign the configuration to your access key.

### 5. Send requests

```python Python theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1",
    api_key="ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="azure-openai:gpt-4o",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)
```

```typescript TypeScript theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
import OpenAI from "openai";

const client = new OpenAI({
  baseURL: "https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1",
  apiKey: "ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx"
});

const response = await client.chat.completions.create({
  model: "azure-openai:gpt-4o",
  messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Hello!" }]
});

console.log(response.choices[0].message.content);
```

## Multiple deployments and regions

Create a separate custom provider for each Azure deployment or region.
Give each a unique provider ID (for example `azure-gpt4`, `azure-eastus`) with its own deployment URL and model list.

Attach the same or different provider keys per deployment.
Pin a region with `azure-eastus:gpt-4o`, or list multiple models for failover: `models: ["azure-eastus:gpt-4o", "openai:gpt-4o"]`.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Fix |
| - | - |
| 401 unauthorized | Verify the provider key in app.ngrok.ai matches Azure Portal and is attached in your access key configuration |
| 404 deployment not found | Check the deployment name in the base URL matches Azure Portal |
| API version errors | Update the `api-version` query parameter to a [supported version](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/openai/reference) |
| 429 rate limiting | Add multiple provider keys for failover or request a quota increase in Azure Portal |

# Connect LM Studio to the AI Gateway
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/custom-providers/lm-studio

Connect LM Studio on your machine to ngrok.ai with an ngrok endpoint, so your apps can call your local models through the AI Gateway.

[LM Studio](https://lmstudio.ai) is a desktop app for running LLMs locally with an [OpenAI-compatible API](https://lmstudio.ai/docs/developer/openai-compat).
Connect it to the AI Gateway as a [custom provider](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/custom-providers).

## What you'll need

* [ngrok account](https://app.ngrok.ai) with AI Gateway access
* [LM Studio](https://lmstudio.ai/download) installed
* [ngrok agent](https://download.ngrok.com) installed
* A model downloaded in LM Studio
* An [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys) from [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai)

## Overview

LM Studio runs a local HTTP server.
Expose it with an ngrok internal endpoint, register the endpoint as a custom provider, then route traffic through the gateway.

```mermaid theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
graph LR
    A[Client] --> B[gateway.ngrok.ai]
    B --> C[ngrok Internal Endpoint]
    C --> D[LM Studio localhost:1234]
```

## Getting started

### 1. Start LM Studio's local server

Download a model and start the server:

> [tab] GUI
>
> 1. Open LM Studio and download a model from the **Discover** tab
> 2. Go to **Developer**, select the model, and click **Start Server**

> [tab] CLI
>
> ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
> lms get llama-3.2-3b-instruct@q4_k_m
> lms server start
> ```

By default, LM Studio listens on port `1234`.
Verify the server is running:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
curl http://localhost:1234/v1/models
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> Use the model ID exactly as LM Studio reports it from `GET /v1/models`.

### 2. Expose LM Studio with ngrok

Create an [internal endpoint](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-a-model-you-run-yourself#connect-a-local-model-with-an-internal-endpoint):

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
ngrok http 1234 --url https://lm-studio.internal
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> Internal endpoints (`.internal` domains) are private to your ngrok account, meaning they're not reachable from the public internet.
> Use the same ngrok account here and in the AI Gateway, otherwise the gateway can't reach the endpoint.

### 3. Create the custom provider

See [Create a custom provider](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-a-model-you-run-yourself#create-a-custom-provider).
Use provider ID `lm-studio`, base URL `https://lm-studio.internal`, and your model IDs.

> [!TIP]
>
> LM Studio doesn't require upstream authentication, so you can skip provider keys.

### 4. Configure access

Create an [access key configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations) that allows the `lm-studio` provider, then assign it to your access key.

### 5. Send requests

```python Python theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1",
    api_key="ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="lm-studio:llama-3.2-3b-instruct",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)
```

```typescript TypeScript theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
const response = await client.chat.completions.create({
```

## Tips

* **Embeddings**: To send `/v1/embeddings` requests through the gateway, add `{ "format": "openai", "surface": "embeddings" }` to the provider's `supportedApiSurfaces`, and add your embedding model's ID to its models.
* **Slow first response**: Pre-load the model in LM Studio or enable **Keep model in memory** in settings.
  Increase `perRequestTimeout` in [account settings](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/account-settings) if needed.
* **Cloud fallback**: Add a built-in provider to your access key configuration and use `models: ["lm-studio:llama-3.2-3b-instruct", "openai:gpt-4o"]` for failover.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Fix |
| - | - |
| Connection refused | Confirm the LM Studio server is running and the ngrok tunnel is active |
| Model not found | Check `curl http://localhost:1234/v1/models` and match the model ID exactly |
| Out of memory | Use a smaller model or lower quantization (Q4 instead of Q8) |
| Port in use | Change the port in LM Studio settings and update your ngrok command |

# Connect Ollama to the AI Gateway
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/custom-providers/ollama

Connect Ollama on your machine to ngrok.ai with an ngrok endpoint, so your apps can call your local models through the AI Gateway.

[Ollama](https://ollama.ai) runs open-source large language models locally.
This guide shows you how to connect Ollama to the ngrok AI Gateway as a [custom provider](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/custom-providers).

## What you'll need

* [ngrok account](https://app.ngrok.ai) with AI Gateway access
* [Ollama](https://ollama.ai/download) installed locally
* [ngrok agent](https://download.ngrok.com) installed
* An [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys) from [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai)

## Overview

Ollama runs on HTTP locally.
Expose it with an ngrok internal endpoint, register the endpoint as a custom provider, then route traffic through the gateway.

```mermaid theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
graph LR
    A[Client] --> B[gateway.ngrok.ai]
    B --> C[ngrok Internal Endpoint]
    C --> D[Ollama localhost:11434]
```

## Getting started

### 1. Start Ollama

Start the Ollama server:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
ollama serve
```

Pull a model if you haven't already:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
ollama pull llama3.2
```

Verify Ollama is running:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
curl http://localhost:11434/api/tags
```

### 2. Expose Ollama with ngrok

Create an [internal endpoint](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-a-model-you-run-yourself#connect-a-local-model-with-an-internal-endpoint) with the [ngrok agent](/docs/gateway/agent/):

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
ngrok http 11434 --url https://ollama.internal
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> Internal endpoints (`.internal` domains) are private to your ngrok account, meaning they're not reachable from the public internet.
> Use the same ngrok account here and in the AI Gateway, otherwise the gateway can't reach the endpoint.

### 3. Create the custom provider

See [Create a custom provider](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-a-model-you-run-yourself#create-a-custom-provider).
Use provider ID `ollama`, base URL `https://ollama.internal`, and your model IDs (for example `llama3.2`).

> [!TIP]
>
> Ollama doesn't require upstream authentication, so you can skip provider keys.

### 4. Configure access

Create an [access key configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations) that allows your `ollama` provider, then assign it to your access key.
See the [Quickstart](/docs/ai-gateway/quickstart) if you haven't created an access key yet.

### 5. Send requests

Point any OpenAI-compatible SDK at the gateway using your access key:

```python Python theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1",
    api_key="ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="ollama:llama3.2",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)
```

```typescript TypeScript theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
import OpenAI from "openai";

const client = new OpenAI({
  baseURL: "https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1",
  apiKey: "ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx"
});

const response = await client.chat.completions.create({
  model: "ollama:llama3.2",
  messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Hello!" }]
});

console.log(response.choices[0].message.content);
```

```bash cURL theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
curl https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx" \
  -d '{
    "model": "ollama:llama3.2",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]
  }'
```

## Tips

* **Slow first response**: Ollama loads models into memory on first use.
  Increase `perRequestTimeout` in [account settings](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/account-settings) if requests time out during warm-up.
* **Multiple instances**: Create separate custom providers (for example `ollama-gpu-1`, `ollama-gpu-2`) with different internal endpoints.
  Pin a request with `ollama-gpu-1:llama3.2` or list multiple models for failover.
* **Cloud fallback**: Add a built-in provider to your access key configuration and request `models: ["ollama:llama3.2", "openai:gpt-4o"]` for cross-provider failover.
  See [Multi-provider failover](/docs/ai-gateway/examples/multi-provider-failover).

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Fix |
| - | - |
| Connection refused | Confirm Ollama is running (`curl http://localhost:11434/api/tags`) and the ngrok tunnel is active |
| Model not found | Run `ollama list`, pull the model, and match the model ID exactly (including tags like `:1b`) |
| Out of memory | Use a smaller or quantized model, or set `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1` |

* [Use a model you run yourself](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-a-model-you-run-yourself): URL requirements and local networking
* [Access Key Configurations](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations): Scope providers per key
* [Quickstart](/docs/ai-gateway/quickstart): Create your first access key


# Connect vLLM to the AI Gateway
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/custom-providers/vllm

Connect your vLLM server to ngrok.ai with an ngrok endpoint, so your apps can call your self-hosted models through the AI Gateway.

[vLLM](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm) is a high-performance inference engine with an OpenAI-compatible API.
Connect your vLLM server to the AI Gateway as a [custom provider](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/custom-providers).

## What you'll need

* [ngrok account](https://app.ngrok.ai) with AI Gateway access
* [vLLM](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/getting_started/installation.html) installed
* [ngrok agent](https://download.ngrok.com) installed
* GPU with sufficient VRAM for your chosen model
* An [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys) from [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai)

## Overview

vLLM provides an OpenAI-compatible server that you can expose with an ngrok internal endpoint (or use a public HTTPS URL), register as a custom provider, and attach credentials through an access key configuration.

```mermaid theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
graph LR
    A[Client] --> B[gateway.ngrok.ai]
    B --> C[ngrok Internal Endpoint]
    C --> D[vLLM Server :8000]
```

## Getting started

### 1. Start vLLM

Start the OpenAI-compatible server:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.2-8B-Instruct
```

Verify it's running:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
curl http://localhost:8000/v1/models
```

### 2. Expose with ngrok

Create an [internal endpoint](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-a-model-you-run-yourself#connect-a-local-model-with-an-internal-endpoint):

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
ngrok http 8000 --url https://vllm.internal
```

If vLLM already has a public HTTPS endpoint, skip this step and use that URL as the provider base URL instead.

### 3. Create the custom provider

See [Create a custom provider](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-a-model-you-run-yourself#create-a-custom-provider).
Use provider ID `vllm`, base URL `https://vllm.internal`, API format **OpenAI Chat Completions**, and your model IDs.

### 4. Store a provider key (if required)

If your vLLM server requires an API key (`vllm serve model --api-key your-secret-key`), [add a provider key](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/attaching-provider-keys#add-a-provider-key).

### 5. Configure access

Create an [access key configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations) that:

1. Allows the `vllm` provider in the access scope
2. Adds a routing rule with **Bring your own API key** if the server requires authentication

Assign the configuration to your access key.

### 6. Send requests

```python Python theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1",
    api_key="ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="vllm:meta-llama/Llama-3.2-8B-Instruct",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)
```

```typescript TypeScript theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
import OpenAI from "openai";

const client = new OpenAI({
  baseURL: "https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1",
  apiKey: "ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx"
});

const response = await client.chat.completions.create({
  model: "vllm:meta-llama/Llama-3.2-8B-Instruct",
  messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Hello!" }]
});

console.log(response.choices[0].message.content);
```

## Tips

* **Secure vLLM**: Run with `--api-key` and attach the key through an [access key configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations).
  The AI Gateway adds it to upstream requests server-side.
* **Gated models**: Set `HF_TOKEN` before starting vLLM for Hugging Face gated models.
* **Timeouts**: Large models can be slow.
  Increase `perRequestTimeout` and `totalTimeout` in [account settings](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/account-settings).
* **Multiple models**: Run separate vLLM instances with different internal endpoints and register each as its own custom provider.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Fix |
| - | - |
| Model loading errors | Check GPU memory with `nvidia-smi`; try `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.9` or a smaller model |
| Connection timeouts | Verify the ngrok tunnel and vLLM health (`curl http://localhost:8000/health`); increase gateway timeouts |
| 401 unauthorized | Confirm the provider key in app.ngrok.ai matches your vLLM `--api-key` and is attached in the access key configuration |
