# Upload and Use Files
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/guides/files

Stop resending large documents and images with every prompt by storing them with the OpenAI or Anthropic Files API through ngrok.ai.

Use the Files API when you want to upload a document or image once and reference it by ID in later requests, instead of sending the bytes inline every time.

The AI Gateway serves the OpenAI and Anthropic Files APIs at `https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1/files`.
The request and response shapes match the provider's own API, so the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs work with one extra header.

## Endpoints

| Method | Path | Description |
| - | - | - |
| `POST` | `/v1/files` | Upload a file. The body is `multipart/form-data`. |
| `GET` | `/v1/files` | List files. |
| `GET` | `/v1/files/{file_id}` | Get a file's metadata. |
| `GET` | `/v1/files/{file_id}/content` | Download a file's contents. |
| `DELETE` | `/v1/files/{file_id}` | Delete a file. |

## Name the provider

A file request has no model, so the gateway can't work out the provider on its own.
Every Files API request must send the `Ngrok-AIG-Provider` header:

| Provider | Header value |
| - | - |
| OpenAI | `Ngrok-AIG-Provider: openai` |
| Anthropic | `Ngrok-AIG-Provider: anthropic` |

The gateway removes this header before it calls the provider.
Other providers, including Google, aren't supported.

The access key's [configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations) must allow the provider.

## Upload and use a file

Upload the file, then reference its ID in a request to a model from the same provider.
A file ID only means something to the provider that stored it.

```python OpenAI Python highlight={11} theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1",
    api_key="ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx",  # Your access key
)

uploaded = client.files.create(
    file=open("report.pdf", "rb"),
    purpose="user_data",
    extra_headers={"Ngrok-AIG-Provider": "openai"},
)

response = client.responses.create(
    model="openai:gpt-5.4",
    input=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {"type": "input_file", "file_id": uploaded.id},
                {"type": "input_text", "text": "Summarize this report in three bullets."},
            ],
        }
    ],
)

print(response.output_text)
```

```typescript OpenAI TypeScript highlight={10} theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
import fs from "node:fs";
import OpenAI from "openai";

const client = new OpenAI({
  baseURL: "https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1",
  apiKey: "ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx", // Your access key
});

const uploaded = await client.files.create(
  { file: fs.createReadStream("report.pdf"), purpose: "user_data" },
  { headers: { "Ngrok-AIG-Provider": "openai" } },
);

const response = await client.responses.create({
  model: "openai:gpt-5.4",
  input: [
    {
      role: "user",
      content: [
        { type: "input_file", file_id: uploaded.id },
        { type: "input_text", text: "Summarize this report in three bullets." },
      ],
    },
  ],
});

console.log(response.output_text);
```

```python Anthropic Python highlight={10} theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic(
    base_url="https://gateway.ngrok.ai",
    api_key="ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx",  # Your access key
)

uploaded = client.beta.files.upload(
    file=("report.pdf", open("report.pdf", "rb"), "application/pdf"),
    extra_headers={"Ngrok-AIG-Provider": "anthropic"},
)

message = client.beta.messages.create(
    model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    betas=["files-api-2025-04-14"],
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {"type": "document", "source": {"type": "file", "file_id": uploaded.id}},
                {"type": "text", "text": "Summarize this report in three bullets."},
            ],
        }
    ],
)

print(message.content[0].text)
```

```bash curl theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
curl https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1/files \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx" \
  -H "Ngrok-AIG-Provider: openai" \
  -F purpose="user_data" \
  -F file="@report.pdf"
```

The Anthropic SDK takes the base URL without `/v1`.
The gateway adds the `files-api-2025-04-14` beta flag to Anthropic file requests for you, and keeps any other beta flags you send.

Pass `Ngrok-AIG-Provider` on each file call rather than as a client default header, since inference requests don't need it.

Files work in these request types:

| Endpoint | Where the file ID goes |
| - | - |
| Chat Completions (`/v1/chat/completions`) | A `file` content part: `{"type": "file", "file": {"file_id": "..."}}` |
| Responses (`/v1/responses`) | An `input_file` content part, or a code interpreter tool's `container.file_ids` |
| Messages (`/v1/messages`) | A `document` or `image` block with `"source": {"type": "file", "file_id": "..."}` |

## Paying with credits or your own key

The gateway picks credentials for a file request the same way it does for a model request to that provider: from the [routing rule](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations) in the access key's configuration.
If the access key has no configuration, or the configuration has no rule for that provider, the gateway uses your stored [provider key](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/attaching-provider-keys) when you have one, and [credits](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/pay-with-credits) otherwise.

Each request uses one credential and doesn't switch partway. A file stored with your own key lives in your provider account, and a file uploaded with credits lives with ngrok.ai, so they're never mixed.

Upload files and send the requests that use them with the same access key, so both go through the same credentials.
To be sure, add a routing rule for the provider to the access key's configuration.

### With your own provider key

Requests go straight through to your provider account:

* Listing returns every file in your provider account, including files you uploaded outside the gateway.
* You can reference any file your provider account holds.
* Expiry, retention, and storage limits are the provider's own.

### When you pay with credits

ngrok.ai stores the file under an ngrok.ai account at the provider and keeps track of which files belong to your account:

* **Expiry**: Files expire 72 hours after upload. On OpenAI, any `expires_after` you send is replaced with that 72-hour expiry.
* **Storage limit**: Your account can hold up to 5 GB of files per provider. Delete files you no longer need to free up room. Expired files stop counting once they're removed, shortly after they expire.
* **Listing**: Listing only returns files your account uploaded with credits. Pages hold at most 100 files. Follow the cursor in the response (`after` for OpenAI, `after_id` for Anthropic) to read the rest. OpenAI's `order=asc` and Anthropic's `before_id` aren't supported.
* **Using files**: A request can only reference files your account uploaded with credits. If a request references any other file ID, the gateway won't use credits for that model. It uses your own provider key for that provider if one is routed, and otherwise returns [`ERR_NGROK_27240`](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/error-codes#err_ngrok_27240).

## Limits

* **File size**: An upload can be at most 512 MiB, whichever credentials it uses.
* **Timeout**: A transfer must finish within your account's total timeout, 120 seconds by default. Raise it in [Account Settings](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/account-settings) for large files on slow connections.
* **Credits**: Uploads, listings, metadata, and downloads need a positive [credit](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/credits) balance, but they don't spend credits. Deletes work at a zero balance, so you can always free storage.

## Errors

File errors use the provider's error format, so your SDK raises its usual exception. A request that doesn't name a provider gets the OpenAI format.

| Code | Status | What happened |
| - | - | - |
| `ERR_NGROK_27240` | 404 | A model request referenced files your account didn't upload with credits. |
| `ERR_NGROK_27241` | 400 | The request is missing the `Ngrok-AIG-Provider` header. |
| `ERR_NGROK_27242` | 400 | The provider in `Ngrok-AIG-Provider` doesn't support the Files API. |
| `ERR_NGROK_27243` | 400 | The list `limit` isn't a whole number from 1 to 100. |
| `ERR_NGROK_27244` | 404 | Your account has no file with that ID for that provider. |
| `ERR_NGROK_27245` | 400 | A list parameter isn't supported when you pay with credits, such as OpenAI's `order=asc` or Anthropic's `before_id`. |
| `ERR_NGROK_27246` | 413 | The upload would put your account over its storage limit for that provider. |
| `ERR_NGROK_27247` | 400 | The upload isn't a `multipart/form-data` request. |
| `ERR_NGROK_27248` | 413 | The upload is larger than 512 MiB. |

See [Error codes](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/error-codes) for every gateway error.

# Guard Agent Tool Calls with Firewall
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/guides/firewall-policies

Use an ngrok.ai Firewall policy to block risky AI agent tool calls, like a force-push, and test it before you enforce it.

In this guide, you create a [Firewall](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/firewall) policy that stops your agents from force-pushing, test it on one request, watch what it catches in Dry run, and then enforce it on your access keys.

## What you'll need

* An [ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai) account and an [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys).
* An agent or app that calls `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/responses`, `/v1/messages`, or Gemini `generateContent` through the gateway with tools.
* To apply a policy to some keys and not others, an [access key configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations) for those keys.

## 1. Create a policy

1. In [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai), go to **Firewall** and click **New firewall policy**.
2. Enter a **Name**, such as `Coding agent guard`.
3. Under **Mode**, select **Dry run**.
   New policies start in **Enforce**, so switch now and enforce after you've tested.
4. Under **On error**, keep **Block** to block what Firewall can't check once you enforce, or select **Continue** to let it through.

## 2. Add rules

The new policy comes with one example rule under **Response rules**.
Edit it or remove it, then click **Add rule** for each rule you need.

For each rule, pick:

* **Rule name**: a short description.
  The agent sees it when the rule blocks something, so make it clear, such as `Force push`.
* **Type**: **Tool names**, **Regex**, or **Decision**.
  See [Rule types](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/firewall#rule-types).
* **Tier**: **Hard block**, **Soft block**, or **Allow**.
  See [Tiers](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/firewall#tiers).
* **Reads**: for a request rule, which parts of the request the rule reads.

Put a rule under **Request rules** to check what the agent sends before it reaches the model.
Put it under **Response rules** to check each tool call the model returns.

For a decision rule, describe what to catch in plain language, and leave **Min. confidence %** empty to use the default: 60 for a block rule and 70 for an allow rule.
Raise it if the rule blocks too often, and lower it if it misses things.

Under **Environment details**, add facts that help decision rules judge a call, such as `Deploy target: staging only` or `Trusted repo: github.com/acme/app`.
Environment details aren't rules, so they never block anything by themselves.

### Example rules

| Goal | Rule | Match |
| - | - | - |
| Block force pushes | Response rule, Regex, Hard block | `git push .*(--force\|-f)\b` |
| Block deleting the whole filesystem | Response rule, Regex, Hard block | `rm -rf /["\s]` |
| Stop pushes to the wrong repo | Response rule, Decision, Hard block, with the environment detail `Trusted repo: github.com/acme/app` | "Pushes code to a repository other than the trusted repo." |
| Stop agents from sending AWS keys | Response rule, Regex, Hard block | `AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}` |
| Block a whole MCP server | Response rule, Tool names, Hard block | `mcp__payments__*` |
| Block requests that offer a tool | Request rule that reads **Tool definitions**, Tool names, Hard block | `delete_*` |
| Stop destructive commands nobody asked for | Response rule, Decision, Soft block | "Deletes files, drops databases, or rewrites history, and the user didn't ask for it." |
| Allow cleanup of the build folder | Response rule, Regex, Allow | `rm -rf \./build/` |
| Catch prompt injection in fetched pages | Request rule that reads **Tool results**, Decision, Hard block | "Text that tells the assistant to ignore its instructions or to send data somewhere." |
| Catch AWS keys in tool output | Request rule that reads **Tool results**, Regex, Hard block | `AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}` |

Regex rules are case-sensitive.
Start a pattern with `(?i)` to ignore case.

Click **Create policy** to save it.

## 3. Try it in one request

Before you apply the policy to any keys, test it on a single request.
Under **Try it in one request**, the policy editor shows a `plugins` field that carries the same rules.
Add it to the body of a chat completions or messages request, and the gateway checks that request with those rules.

This request offers the model a `bash` tool and asks it to push, so the model returns a tool call for the rule to check:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
curl https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $NGROK_AI_ACCESS_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "gpt-4o",
    "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "Force push my changes to main." }],
    "tools": [{
      "type": "function",
      "function": {
        "name": "bash",
        "description": "Run a shell command.",
        "parameters": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": { "command": { "type": "string" } },
          "required": ["command"]
        }
      }
    }],
    "plugins": [{
      "id": "firewall",
      "mode": "enforce",
      "on_error": "block",
      "classifier_context": {
        "v": 1,
        "auto_mode": {
          "hard_deny": [{
            "id": "force-push",
            "name": "Force push",
            "kind": "regex",
            "pattern": "git push .*(--force|-f)\\b"
          }]
        }
      }
    }]
  }'
```

If the model calls `bash` with a force push, the response still returns `200`, but the tool call is gone.
In its place, the assistant message says the call was blocked, `finish_reason` is `stop`, and `safeguard_results` reports the verdict:

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "choices": [{
    "message": {
      "role": "assistant",
      "content": "<ngrok_firewall_blocked tool=\"bash\" rule=\"[Force push]\">Tool call \"bash\" was blocked by ngrok.ai Firewall and was not executed. Do not retry it with the same arguments.</ngrok_firewall_blocked>"
    },
    "finish_reason": "stop"
  }],
  "safeguard_results": [{
    "type": "dangerous_tool_use",
    "status": {
      "type": "available",
      "tool_uses": {
        "call_abc123": { "type": "evaluated", "outcome": "flagged", "explanation": "[Force push]" }
      }
    }
  }]
}
```

The response is trimmed to the fields Firewall changes.
Change `mode` to `audit` to see what Dry run reports: the tool call comes back unchanged, and `safeguard_results` still shows `flagged`.

See the [Firewall reference](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/firewall) for the full `plugins` format and every response field.

## 4. Apply the policy to keys

Open the policy, find **Apply to**, and pick one:

* **All access keys**: the policy becomes your baseline and checks every key in your account, including keys you create later.
  Your account has one baseline, so this replaces the current one.
* **Only these configurations**: the policy checks keys that use the configurations you pick.

Click **Save changes**.
Saved changes reach the gateway within seconds.

You can also pick the policy from an access key configuration.
Open the configuration, go to its **Firewall** section, and select the policy under **Policy**.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Policies combine.
> A key whose configuration picks a policy is also checked by your baseline.
> Each policy keeps its own mode, so a Dry run policy only reports, even next to an enforced baseline.
> See [How policies combine](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/firewall#how-policies-combine).

## 5. Watch, tune, and enforce

While the policy is in Dry run, check what it would block:

* Read the `Ngrok-AIG-Firewall-Request` header for request rules, such as `flagged; rules=prompt-injection`.
* Read `safeguard_results` in the response body for both request rules and tool calls.

When a rule flags calls it shouldn't, raise its confidence, narrow its pattern, or add an allow rule next to a soft block rule.
When the results look right, open the policy, select **Enforce** under **Mode**, and click **Save changes**.

> [!WARNING]
>
> Once a key has an enforced policy with **On error** set to **Block**, the gateway rejects that key's requests to endpoints Firewall can't check, such as the Gemini Interactions API.
> Use a separate key for those requests, or set **On error** to **Continue** to let them through unchecked.

## Use the API instead

You can do every step in this guide with the [AI Gateway API](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/overview).
Authorize each request with your [AI Gateway API key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys#credentials-overview).

Create a policy with the [Firewall Policies API](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/firewall-policies/create).
The API uses the same fields as the dashboard, and each rule sets its own `tier`:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
curl -X POST https://api.ngrok.ai/firewall-policies \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "Coding agent guard",
    "mode": "audit",
    "onError": "block",
    "rules": [
      {
        "id": "force-push",
        "name": "Force push",
        "tier": "hardDeny",
        "kind": "regex",
        "pattern": "git push .*(--force|-f)\\b"
      }
    ]
  }'
```

Attach the policy to an access key configuration:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
curl -X PATCH https://api.ngrok.ai/access-key-configurations/aigac_xxxxx \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "firewallPolicyId": "aigfp_xxxxx" }'
```

Send `"firewallPolicyId": null` to detach it.

Or make it your baseline with the [gateway configuration API](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/gateway-config/update).
Send `expectedFirewallPolicyId` with the baseline you read, or `null` if you expect none, so the update fails with a `409` instead of replacing a baseline someone else just set:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
curl -X PATCH https://api.ngrok.ai/gateway-config \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "firewallPolicyId": "aigfp_xxxxx", "expectedFirewallPolicyId": null }'
```

To enforce the policy, [update it](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/firewall-policies/update) with `"mode": "enforce"`.

# Configure Provider Key Failover
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/guides/key-selection-failover

Add backup provider keys so the AI Gateway can retry with another key when one is rate limited or out of quota.

Configure multiple provider keys in an [access key configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations) routing rule. The gateway tries keys in order when one hits a rate limit, runs out of quota, or fails authentication.

## How failover works

When a routing rule step lists multiple provider keys:

1. The gateway tries the first key.
2. On a rate limit (429), or an auth failure (401 or 403) because the provider rejected the key, it tries the next key.
3. When no keys are left, the gateway falls back to paying with credits if the rule has an `ngrok` step after this one. Otherwise it moves to the next model you listed, or returns the last error.

Server errors (5xx), timeouts, and connection failures don't try the next key. Another key for the same provider would likely fail the same way, so the gateway moves straight to the next model you listed. To fail over on those errors, add [fallback models](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/configure-fallback-models).

Failover is configured per provider in the access key configuration—not in your application code.

## Via dashboard

1. [Add multiple provider keys](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/attaching-provider-keys#add-a-provider-key) for the same provider.
2. [Edit an access key configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations#create-a-configuration).
3. Add or edit a routing rule for the provider.
4. Attach multiple keys to the **Bring your own API key** step in the order you want them tried.

## Via the AI Gateway API

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
curl -X POST https://api.ngrok.ai/access-key-configurations \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "OpenAI with failover",
    "router": {
      "rules": [
        {
          "provider": "openai",
          "steps": [
            {
              "type": "user",
              "keySelectionStrategy": "ordered",
              "keys": [
                { "id": "aigpk_primary" },
                { "id": "aigpk_backup" }
              ]
            }
          ]
        }
      ]
    }
  }'
```

See the [Access Key Configurations API reference](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/access-key-configurations/create).

Assign the configuration to your access key. Your app sends only the access key:

```python theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1",
    api_key="ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx",
)
```

# Choose a Model
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/guides/model-selection-strategies

Compare the ways to pick a model in an AI Gateway request, whether you name the model or provider yourself or let ngrok.ai choose.

When you send a request to `https://gateway.ngrok.ai`, the `model` field tells the AI Gateway which model to call.

Use a model ID when you want the gateway to resolve the provider from the [model catalog](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/model-catalog). Use `provider:model` when you want to choose the provider yourself.

## Use a model ID

Use a model ID when you know which model you want to call and don't need to force a specific provider.

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "model": "gpt-4o",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
}
```

The gateway looks up `gpt-4o` in the [model catalog](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/model-catalog) and finds every provider that serves it. It tries the model author's own provider first (OpenAI here), then any reseller that serves the same model, such as OpenRouter. Providers your access key can't use drop out.

## Route to a specific provider

Use `provider:model` when you want predictable routing or need to avoid ambiguity between model names.

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "model": "openai:gpt-4o",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
}
```

In this example:

* `openai` is the provider ID.
* `gpt-4o` is the model ID.

Use this format when you have more than one provider configured, want to call a custom provider, or want the request to go to one specific upstream.

## Let ngrok.ai choose

Set `model` to `ngrok/auto` to let ngrok.ai pick a model for each request, starting with the cheapest one that fits the prompt. See [Automatic model selection](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/automatic-model-selection).

## Use a custom provider model

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "model": "my-ollama:llama3.2",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
}
```

Custom providers use the same `provider:model` format. In this example, `my-ollama` is your custom provider ID and `llama3.2` is the model ID configured on that provider.

## Check model capabilities

Before choosing a model, check the [model catalog](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/model-catalog) for:

| Field | Use it to check |
| - | - |
| Context window | How much input the model can accept |
| Output tokens | How much output the model can return |
| Modalities | Whether the model supports text, image, audio, video, or files |
| Provider key required | Whether you need to bring your own provider key |

## Keep access rules in mind

The request can only use providers and models allowed by the [access key configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations) assigned to the access key.

If you need to limit what a client can call, see [Restrict providers and models](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/restrict-providers-and-models).

# Pay with Credits
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/guides/pay-with-credits

Call OpenAI, Anthropic, and other supported models through ngrok.ai with only an access key, and learn how credits cover the model cost.

Pay with credits when you want the AI Gateway to supply the provider credentials for you, so you don't need a provider account.

Your app sends an [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys) to the gateway.
The gateway authenticates to the supported upstream provider, and credits cover the model cost plus the gateway processing fee.

> [!NOTE]
>
> You can pay with credits for models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek, xAI, Moonshot AI, Z.ai, and other built-in providers.
> Availability is per model; the [model catalog](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/model-catalog#billing-and-provider-credentials) shows which providers support it.
> For providers that require your own credentials, [bring your own provider key](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/attaching-provider-keys).

## What you'll need

* An ngrok account.
* An [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys) from [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai).
* Credits in your AI Gateway account.

## Create an access key

Create an access key in [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai).
Use this key as the API key in your SDK.

The access key authenticates your application to the gateway.
It's different from a provider key, which authenticates the gateway to an upstream provider.

## Call a supported OpenAI model

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "model": "openai:gpt-4o",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
}
```

You can also use the model ID directly:

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "model": "gpt-4o",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
}
```

## Call a supported Anthropic model

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "model": "anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
}
```

## How billing works

When you pay with credits, credits cover:

* The upstream model cost.
* [Hosted tools](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/hosted-tools) the provider bills, such as web search, code execution, and image generation.
* The AI Gateway processing fee.

Before sending a request, the gateway checks that you can pay for it with credits.
If you can't pay for a model or feature with credits, you get an error asking you to add your own provider key.
See [`ERR_NGROK_27238`](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/error-codes#err_ngrok_27238).

For providers or models you can't pay for with credits, or when you want your provider to bill usage directly, [bring your own provider key](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/attaching-provider-keys).

## When to bring your own key instead

Bring your own provider key when:

* You already have a provider account.
* You want your provider to bill usage directly.
* You have negotiated provider pricing.
* You need a provider or model that requires your own credentials.

# Compare Models in the Playground
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/guides/playground

Send one prompt to up to three models in the app.ngrok.ai playground and compare their streamed answers side by side.

The playground in [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai/playground) sends prompts through the AI Gateway from your browser.
Use it to try a model before you write any code, or to send the same prompt to up to three models and compare their answers side by side as they stream in.

Playground requests are real gateway requests.
They use one of your [access keys](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys), they're billed like any other request, and they appear on the [Activity](https://app.ngrok.ai/activity) page.

## What you'll need

* An ngrok account. Sign in at [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai).
* [Credits](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/credits) in your AI Gateway account. Every request needs a positive balance, including requests that use your own provider keys.

## Open the playground

Select **Playground** in the app.ngrok.ai sidebar.

From any other page, you can open the playground as a side panel with the playground button in the page header.
Select **Open page** in the panel to switch to the full page.
The panel and the page show the same conversation.

## Compare models

The playground starts with one model selected. Its chip sits at the bottom of the message box, next to the key icon.

1. Select the key icon to choose an access key.
   Every model uses this key unless you [override it](#configure-each-model).
2. Select **+** (**Add model**) and pick a model to compare.
   Repeat to add a third model.
3. Type a prompt and press **Enter**, or select **Send message**.

Each model answers in its own column, streamed as tokens arrive.
Follow-up prompts go to every enabled model, and each model keeps its own conversation history.

![Playground in app.ngrok.ai with GPT-5.6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 answering the same prompt side by side, and both model chips in the message box](https://mintcdn.com/ngrok/NtlJmMH9rvSW0IRo/ai-gateway/guides/img/playground-compare-models.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=NtlJmMH9rvSW0IRo\&q=85\&s=9d613b97313082c347db24a8c5df2efd)

The model list shows only models the access key can use.
If the key has an [access key configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations) that restricts providers or models, the rest are left out.

## Configure each model

Select a model's chip in the message box to open its settings:

| Setting | What it does |
| - | - |
| **Enable model** | Turn off to stop sending new prompts to this model. Its earlier answers stay in the conversation. |
| **Primary model** | Switch this column to another model. |
| **Fallbacks** | Select **Add fallback** to add [fallback models](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/configure-fallback-models) the gateway tries, in order, if the primary model fails. |
| **Override access key** | Send this model's requests with a different access key than the rest. |
| **Enable system prompt** | Add a system prompt for this model only. |

Models that support reasoning also show a thinking effort or budget setting, and models that can create images show image generation settings.

![Settings for one model in the playground, with Enable model, Primary model, Fallbacks with an Add fallback button, Generate images, Override access key, and Enable system prompt](https://mintcdn.com/ngrok/NtlJmMH9rvSW0IRo/ai-gateway/guides/img/playground-model-settings.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=NtlJmMH9rvSW0IRo\&q=85\&s=0f02103b852ce8a1777a9097f400564d)

## See what the gateway did

Select the **Response details** icon under an answer, or hover over it, to see:

* A timing waterfall with the time to the first token and the total time.
* The input and output tokens, when the model reports them.
* Which model answered, when a fallback answered for the primary model.
* **View in Activity**, which opens the request in the [request details panel](/docs/ai-gateway/observability/index#inspect-a-request-in-app-ngrok-ai) with its attempts, timing, and cost.

## Get the code

To make the same request from your app, open the **Playground actions** menu and select **Get code**.
The snippet reproduces the conversation with the first model, including its fallbacks.

## If your balance runs out

When your credit balance reaches \$0, the gateway rejects new requests, so the playground is covered by a **Purchase credits** form.
Pick an amount and complete the purchase. When your credits arrive, the form closes and you can send prompts again.
If you haven't saved a card yet, you add one in Stripe first, then return to the playground and confirm the purchase there. Saving a card doesn't charge you or add credits by itself.

![Purchase credits form covering the playground, with amounts from \$5 to \$100, a note that credits expire after 365 days, and an Add payment method button](https://mintcdn.com/ngrok/NtlJmMH9rvSW0IRo/ai-gateway/guides/img/playground-purchase-credits.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=NtlJmMH9rvSW0IRo\&q=85\&s=da7e71a3af7ec27b19b47727b5280c06)

See [Purchasing credits](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/credits#purchasing-credits) for amounts and limits.

To avoid running out, turn on [automatic top-up](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/credits#automatic-top-up).

## Limits

* **Models**: up to three models per prompt.
* **Access keys**: the access key menu lists only keys whose value ngrok.ai has stored, which is every key created since late July 2026. Older keys don't appear. If you have no usable key, the playground creates one named **Playground Key**.
* **Sessions**: conversations are saved in your browser under **Saved sessions**, not in your ngrok account, so they don't follow you to another browser or device.
* **Billing**: playground requests cost the same as requests from your app and count toward your usage.

# Restrict Providers and Models
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/guides/restrict-providers-and-models

Limit an ngrok.ai access key to specific providers or models so requests for anything else fail right away, including during fallback.

Use access key configurations to control which providers and models an access key can call.

The gateway checks restrictions before it routes a request upstream.
That means a request can fail fast if a client asks for a provider or model the key shouldn't use.

## What you'll need

* An [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys).
* An [access key configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations).
* The provider IDs and model IDs you want to allow.

## Allow specific providers

Use provider restrictions when an access key should only call certain providers.

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "access": {
    "providers": {
      "allow": ["openai", "anthropic"]
    }
  }
}
```

With this configuration, requests can only route to OpenAI or Anthropic.

## Allow specific models

Use model restrictions when an access key should only call certain models.

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "access": {
    "models": {
      "allow": ["openai/gpt-4o", "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6"]
    }
  }
}
```

Model entries accept three forms:

| Entry | Matches |
| - | - |
| `gpt-4o` | The model on any provider that serves it |
| `openai/gpt-4o` | The catalog ID (author and model). Matches that model on any provider that serves it, including resellers such as OpenRouter |
| `openai:openai/gpt-4o` | That model on the `openai` provider only |

Use the `provider:` prefix when you always want to use that provider.
Combine model rules with a provider allowlist to block resellers.

## Allow providers and models together

Combine provider and model restrictions when you want a key to stay within a small set of approved providers and models.

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "access": {
    "providers": {
      "allow": ["openai", "anthropic"]
    },
    "models": {
      "allow": ["openai/gpt-4o", "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6"]
    }
  }
}
```

Requests outside the allowed providers or models are rejected before they reach an upstream provider.

## How this works with fallback

Every model in a fallback request must be allowed.

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "model": "openai:gpt-4o",
  "models": ["anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6"],
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
}
```

If the primary model is allowed but the fallback model isn't, the gateway drops the fallback and names it in the `Ngrok-AIG-Rejected-Models` response header.
The request fails only when none of the models you listed are allowed.

## Virtual models

Model restrictions apply to the models in a [virtual model](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/virtual-models), not to its name.
To let a key use a virtual model, allow the models in it.
The gateway skips each model the key can't use and names it in the `Ngrok-AIG-Rejected-Models` response header.

You can't add a virtual model name to `access.models.allow`.
The API rejects it with the message `'chat-default' is a virtual model. Add its models to the key instead.`

## Common patterns

| Goal | Configuration |
| - | - |
| Allow only OpenAI | Allow provider `openai` |
| Allow only Claude Sonnet | Allow model `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6` |
| Give a team access to two providers | Allow both provider IDs |
| Block expensive models | Allow only approved model IDs |
| Limit a custom provider | Allow the custom provider ID and model IDs |

# Secure Your Gateway
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/guides/securing-endpoints

Give each client its own access key so you can track its usage and revoke it without affecting the others. Clients never hold your provider keys.

[Access keys](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys) authenticate every request to `https://gateway.ngrok.ai`. The AI Gateway validates each key before forwarding traffic. Upstream provider credentials are managed separately—see [Access keys vs provider keys](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys#access-keys-vs-provider-keys).

## How it works

1. [Create an access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys) in [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai) or via the AI Gateway API
2. Send the key as `Authorization: Bearer ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx` (OpenAI-compatible APIs) or `x-api-key` (Anthropic native API)
3. The gateway validates the key on every request
4. Invalid or missing keys are rejected—requests do not reach providers

```python theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1",
    api_key="ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx"  # Your access key
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]
)
```

The AI Gateway replaces your access key with provider credentials from your configuration before forwarding to the upstream provider.

## Per-client keys

Create separate access keys for each client or application:

* Revoke one client without affecting others
* Track usage per key
* Assign different [configurations](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations) to limit scope per client

Create access keys with the [Access Keys API](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/access-keys/create). Authorize the request with your [AI Gateway API key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys#credentials-overview).

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
curl -X POST https://api.ngrok.ai/access-keys \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "name": "Production web app" }'
```

Delete access keys with the [Access Keys API](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/access-keys/delete). Authorize the request with your [AI Gateway API key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys#credentials-overview).

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
curl -X DELETE https://api.ngrok.ai/access-keys/aigk_xxxxx \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY"
```

See the [Access Keys API reference](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/access-keys/delete).

> [!CAUTION]
>
> Deletion is permanent.
> Clients using the revoked key receive authentication errors immediately.

## Protecting provider keys

Store provider keys in app.ngrok.ai and reference them in configurations. Clients only ever hold the access key.

See [Provider Keys](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/attaching-provider-keys).

# Use a Model You Run Yourself
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-a-model-you-run-yourself

Connect Ollama, vLLM, LM Studio, or another model server on your network to ngrok.ai as a custom provider and call it with an access key.

Use a custom provider when you want the AI Gateway to call a model running on your machine, private network, or cloud GPU.

Custom providers can point to self-hosted tools like Ollama, vLLM, LM Studio, or any OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible API.

## What you'll need

Your model server must:

1. Expose a supported API surface, such as OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses, or Anthropic Messages.
2. Be reachable from the AI Gateway.
3. Have at least one model ID configured on the provider.

## Connect a local model with an internal endpoint

If your model runs on your machine or private network, expose it with an ngrok internal endpoint.

For example, if your model server listens on port `11434`:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
ngrok http 11434 --url https://my-ollama.internal
```

Use the internal endpoint URL as the custom provider base URL.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Internal endpoints (`.internal` domains) are private to your ngrok account, meaning they're not reachable from the public internet.
> Use the same ngrok account here and in the AI Gateway, otherwise the gateway can't reach the endpoint.

## Create a custom provider

In [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai):

1. Go to **Providers**.
2. Open the **Custom** tab.
3. Select **Add provider**.
4. Choose **External URL** or **Local**.
5. Enter a provider ID, base URL, API format, and model IDs.
6. Add a provider key if the upstream requires authentication.

## Create a custom provider with the API

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
curl -X POST https://api.ngrok.ai/providers \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "providerId": "my-ollama",
    "name": "Local Ollama",
    "baseUrl": "https://my-ollama.internal",
    "supportedApiSurfaces": [
      { "format": "openai", "surface": "chat-completions" }
    ],
    "models": [{ "modelId": "llama3.2" }]
  }'
```

See the [Providers API reference](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/providers/create) for every field.

## Allow the provider on an access key

An access key without a configuration can call a custom provider as soon as you create it. If you haven't added a provider key, the gateway sends the request without credentials. An access key with a configuration can call the provider only when the configuration's access scope allows it.

To route authenticated traffic to the provider, or to control which access keys can call it:

1. Add a provider key if the upstream requires authentication.
2. Create or update an [access key configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations).
3. Allow the custom provider ID.
4. Assign the configuration to an [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys).

## Call the model

Use `provider:model` in the request.

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "model": "my-ollama:llama3.2",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
}
```

## URL requirements

| URL type | Scheme | Example |
| - | - | - |
| External | `https://` only | `https://api.example.com/v1` |
| ngrok internal | `http://` or `https://` | `https://my-ollama.internal` |

HTTP is only allowed for ngrok `.internal` endpoints. External URLs must use HTTPS.

## Next steps

* [Ollama guide](/docs/ai-gateway/custom-providers/ollama): Connect Ollama
* [vLLM guide](/docs/ai-gateway/custom-providers/vllm): Connect vLLM
* [Provider keys](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/attaching-provider-keys): Store upstream credentials
* [Restrict providers and models](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/restrict-providers-and-models): Allow the custom provider on a key


# Use Any Model with Any SDK
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-any-model-with-any-sdk

Call any supported model from the OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gen AI, or AWS SDK, and learn what the AI Gateway translates between API formats.

Each SDK speaks one API format, and each model serves only some formats.
When the model you pick doesn't serve your SDK's format, the AI Gateway translates the request if it can, calls the model in a format it serves, and translates the response back.
Your code, your stream reader, and your tool loop stay the same, and you change only the model.

Translation works with every access key and needs no setup.
You pay the rates of the model that served the request, and translation adds no fee.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Translation is a quick way to reach many models from one SDK, but API formats don't always match feature for feature.
> When the target format has no place for a field or a tool, the gateway removes it or skips the model, as the rest of this page describes.
> For the best compatibility with a model's features, call it from the SDK for the model's own API format.
> The gateway translates only when it has to, and sends a request to the provider as it is whenever the model serves your SDK's format.

## What you'll need

* An [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys) from the [Quickstart](/docs/ai-gateway/quickstart).
* The Anthropic SDK for Python or TypeScript, as shown in [Anthropic SDK](/docs/ai-gateway/sdks/anthropic#installation).

## Call an OpenAI model from the Anthropic SDK

OpenAI models don't serve the Anthropic Messages API, so this request goes through translation.

### 1. Send the request

Set the model to an OpenAI model.
The rest of the request is a normal Messages request.

```python Python highlight={9} theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic(
    base_url="https://gateway.ngrok.ai",
    api_key="ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx"  # Your access key
)

raw = client.messages.with_raw_response.create(
    model="openai:gpt-5.5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]
)
message = raw.parse()

print(raw.headers.get("ngrok-aig-model"))
print(message.content[0].text)
```

```typescript TypeScript highlight={10} theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
import Anthropic from "@anthropic-ai/sdk";

const client = new Anthropic({
  baseURL: "https://gateway.ngrok.ai",
  apiKey: "ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx",  // Your access key
});

const { data: message, response } = await client.messages
  .create({
    model: "openai:gpt-5.5",
    max_tokens: 1024,
    messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Hello!" }],
  })
  .withResponse();

console.log(response.headers.get("ngrok-aig-model"));
console.log(message.content[0].type === "text" ? message.content[0].text : "");
```

### 2. Confirm which model answered

The `Ngrok-AIG-Model` [response header](/docs/ai-gateway/how-it-works#response-headers) names the OpenAI model that served the request.
The body is a Messages response, so `message.content` holds a `text` block as it does for a Claude model.

In [app.ngrok.ai](https://app.ngrok.ai), open the request in [Request details](/docs/ai-gateway/observability/index#inspect-a-request-in-app-ngrok-ai).
The **Attempts** tab marks the attempt as translated, shows the API format the gateway translated it to, and lists the parameters the gateway changed.

Streaming works the same way.
Call `client.messages.stream(...)` with the OpenAI model, and you get Messages stream events.

## Supported API formats

The gateway translates between these formats in both directions, for buffered and streamed requests:

| Format | Endpoint | SDKs |
| - | - | - |
| OpenAI Chat Completions | `/v1/chat/completions` | [OpenAI SDK](/docs/ai-gateway/sdks/openai), [Vercel AI SDK](/docs/ai-gateway/sdks/vercel-ai-sdk), [LangChain](/docs/ai-gateway/sdks/langchain) |
| OpenAI Responses | `/v1/responses` | [OpenAI SDK](/docs/ai-gateway/sdks/openai#supported-endpoints) |
| Anthropic Messages | `/v1/messages` | [Anthropic SDK](/docs/ai-gateway/sdks/anthropic) |
| Gemini generateContent | `/v1beta/models/{model}:generateContent` | [Google Gen AI SDK](/docs/ai-gateway/sdks/google) |
| Bedrock Converse | `/model/{model}/converse` and `/model/{model}/converse-stream` | [AWS SDK](/docs/ai-gateway/providers/bedrock) |

Translation reaches every model in the [model catalog](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/model-catalog) that serves one of these formats.
It also reaches [models you run yourself](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-a-model-you-run-yourself), through the API format you set on the custom provider.

In the [List Models API](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/models/list), `supported_api_formats` lists the formats a provider serves for a model directly.
`translated_api_formats` lists the other formats that reach the model through translation.

## How the gateway picks a format

The gateway decides for each model when it tries that model:

1. If a provider of the model serves your SDK's format, the gateway sends the request as it is, with no translation.
2. If no provider does, the gateway tries the formats the model serves in this order: Anthropic Messages, Gemini generateContent, OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses, then Bedrock Converse.
   It moves to the next format only when it can't translate the request into the one before.

A provider's own format comes first because a compatibility endpoint can drop features such as reasoning signatures and cache hints.
You can't choose the format yourself.

### Fallback models

The gateway checks each [fallback model](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/configure-fallback-models) when it tries that model, so one list can mix providers and formats:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
curl https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1/messages \
  -H "x-api-key: ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6",
    "models": ["openai:gpt-5.5", "google:gemini-3.6-flash"],
    "max_tokens": 1024,
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]
  }'
```

Whichever model serves the request, the response comes back as a Messages response.
If the gateway can't translate the request for one model, it skips that model and tries the next one.

## What translates

The gateway translates these parts of a request:

* System prompts and instructions.
* Text messages and multi-turn conversations.
* Images.
  Converse models take only base64 image data, not an image URL.
* Function tools, tool calls, and tool results.
* Web search, code execution, and remote MCP servers, as [hosted tools](#hosted-tools) describes.
* The settings in the table that follows.

It translates these parts of a response:

* Text, tool calls, and reasoning.
* Web search sources, and the code and results of code execution.
* Streaming events.
* Token usage.
* Stop reasons, such as end of turn, max tokens, and tool use.
* Provider errors.
  The gateway returns the status code and error type your SDK expects for that failure, and keeps the retry hints, so your SDK retries as it does for a native request.

This table shows the name of each translated setting in each format.
A dash means the format has no such setting, so the gateway removes it.

| Setting | Chat Completions | Responses | Messages | generateContent | Converse |
| - | - | - | - | - | - |
| Max output tokens | `max_completion_tokens` or `max_tokens` | `max_output_tokens` | `max_tokens` | `generationConfig.maxOutputTokens` | `inferenceConfig.maxTokens` |
| Temperature | `temperature` | `temperature` | `temperature` | `generationConfig.temperature` | `inferenceConfig.temperature` |
| Top P | `top_p` | `top_p` | `top_p` | `generationConfig.topP` | `inferenceConfig.topP` |
| Top K | — | — | `top_k` | `generationConfig.topK` | — |
| Stop sequences | `stop` | — | `stop_sequences` | `generationConfig.stopSequences` | `inferenceConfig.stopSequences` |
| Seed | `seed` | — | — | `generationConfig.seed` | — |
| JSON output | `response_format` | `text.format` | `output_config.format` | `generationConfig.responseMimeType` and `responseJsonSchema` | Not translated |
| Tools | `tools` | `tools` | `tools` | `tools[].functionDeclarations` | `toolConfig.tools` |
| Tool choice | `tool_choice` | `tool_choice` | `tool_choice` | `toolConfig.functionCallingConfig` | `toolConfig.toolChoice` |
| Parallel tool calls | `parallel_tool_calls` | `parallel_tool_calls` | `tool_choice.disable_parallel_tool_use` | — | — |
| Reasoning effort | `reasoning_effort` | `reasoning.effort` | `output_config.effort` | `generationConfig.thinkingConfig.thinkingLevel` | — |
| Thinking budget | — | — | `thinking.budget_tokens` | `generationConfig.thinkingConfig.thinkingBudget` | — |

The gateway doesn't translate JSON output to or from Converse yet, so a request that asks for JSON output skips Converse models.

### Hosted tools

[Hosted tools](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/hosted-tools) run on the provider's servers.
The gateway translates these hosted tools:

| Tool | Chat Completions | Responses | Messages | generateContent | Converse |
| - | - | - | - | - | - |
| Web search | Some providers, as the rules below describe | `web_search`, `web_search_preview` | `web_search_20250305` and later versions | `google_search` | — |
| Code execution | — | `code_interpreter` | `code_execution_20250522`, from Messages only | `code_execution` | — |
| Remote MCP servers | — | `mcp` | `mcp_servers` with the `mcp_toolset` tool | — | — |

A dash means the format has no such tool, so the gateway skips a model that serves only that format.

These rules apply to translated hosted tools:

* **Web search on Chat Completions models**: Chat Completions has no standard search tool, so only some providers can search.
  The gateway sends the search as `web_search_options` to OpenAI search models, as `browser_search` to Groq, and as a `web_search` tool to Z.ai.
  For Moonshot, the gateway runs Moonshot's search call for the model and bills both calls as one request.
  The gateway skips Chat Completions models from other providers.
* **Search options**: `user_location` and `search_context_size` reach OpenAI models.
  For other targets, the gateway removes them.
  Allowed and blocked domain lists don't translate to Chat Completions or Gemini models, so the gateway skips those models.
* **Search results**: A Messages client gets the sources of a search from another format as a list at the end of the text, not as citation blocks.
  Other clients get citations in their own format, in buffered and streamed responses.
* **Code execution**: Code tools translate only between formats whose tool runs Python.
  Responses and Gemini models reach each other, and a Messages request with `code_execution_20250522` reaches either.
  Claude models run code through Bash, so a translated request with a code tool never reaches a Claude model.
  Your SDK gets the code the model ran and its result as typed items, not as text.
  Files a code run makes, such as charts, don't come back when your format has no place for them.
* **Remote MCP servers**: MCP translates between Responses and Messages, for Claude models that Anthropic serves directly.
  Set `require_approval` to `never`, because the Messages API has no approval step.
  The gateway skips a Messages model when an MCP tool needs your approval.
* **Conversation history**: When you send earlier search results and citations back on the next turn, a model from another provider gets them as plain text.
* **Billing**: Hosted tools bill at the rate of the tool the provider ran, not the tool your SDK named.

Other hosted tools, such as file search, image generation, URL context, Bash, the text editor, and web fetch, don't translate.

## Removed and changed parameters

The gateway removes or changes a parameter when the target format or model can't take it as you sent it.
It lists each parameter it removed or changed in the `Ngrok-AIG-Removed-Params` [response header](/docs/ai-gateway/how-it-works#response-headers), and in the **Attempts** tab of [Request details](/docs/ai-gateway/observability/index#inspect-a-request-in-app-ngrok-ai).
The header doesn't list a value the gateway adds, such as `max_tokens` for a Messages model.

Fields that only one format defines don't translate.
For example, `frequency_penalty`, `logit_bias`, `metadata`, `service_tier`, and Gemini `safetySettings` reach only a model that serves your SDK's format.
For other models, the gateway removes them.

These rules add or change a value:

* **Max tokens on Messages models**: The Messages API requires `max_tokens`.
  If your request doesn't set a limit, the gateway sends the model's maximum output tokens.
  Your account's [max output tokens](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/account-settings) setting still applies.
  Set your own limit if you need responses to stop at the same length on every model.
* **Sampling settings on Messages models**: The gateway lowers a temperature above 1 to 1.
  If you send both `temperature` and `top_p`, the gateway removes `top_p`.
  Claude models refuse `temperature` and `top_k` while thinking is on, and need a `top_p` of 0.95 or more.
  So when a thinking budget or a reasoning effort turns on thinking, the gateway removes `temperature` and `top_k`, and raises a `top_p` below 0.95 to 0.95.
* **Thinking budget on Messages models**: Messages counts thinking inside `max_tokens`.
  When your budget is larger than the output limit, the gateway lowers the budget so the model still has room to answer.
* **Reasoning effort**: The gateway lowers an effort level the target doesn't have, such as `max`, to `high`.
* **Responses models**: The gateway raises a `max_output_tokens` below 16 to 16.
  It also sends `store: false`, because your SDK can't read a stored response back.
* **Tool schemas**: The gateway removes `strict` for formats that have no strict mode, so the model can return arguments that don't match your schema exactly.
  It removes Gemini's `propertyOrdering` for other formats.
* **Image detail**: Only Chat Completions and Responses take an image `detail` setting.
  Other models get the image at their default detail.

Reasoning settings translate in these ways:

* A reasoning effort reaches every model that can reason, except Converse models.
* Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.1 take a thinking budget, not an effort.
  For these models, the gateway turns on thinking with a budget for your effort level: 1,024 tokens for `minimal` and `low`, 4,096 for `medium`, 16,384 for `high`, and 32,000 for `xhigh` and `max`.
  A budget only approximates an effort, so the gateway lists the effort in the header.
* A thinking budget reaches Claude and Gemini models.
  OpenAI and Converse models take no budget, so the gateway removes it.
* Reasoning blocks from an earlier turn go back only to the format that produced them, because a provider rejects another provider's reasoning signature.
  The gateway removes them for any other format.

Prompt caching markers, such as `cache_control`, reach a model only through the Messages API.
For a model the gateway calls in another format, it removes them.
The response stays the same, but the request can cost more, because the provider doesn't cache the prompt where you marked it.

Provider-specific request headers, such as `anthropic-beta` and `OpenAI-Organization`, don't reach a model the gateway translated the request for.

## When the gateway skips a model

The gateway skips a model, without calling it, when it can't translate the request for that model:

* The request has file, document, audio, or video input.
  Only text and images translate.
* The request has an image URL, and the target is a Converse model.
  Send the image as base64 data instead.
* The request has a hosted tool that the target format doesn't have, or that doesn't translate.
  See [hosted tools](#hosted-tools).
* The request sets `max_uses` for web search, and the target is a Gemini, Groq, or Z.ai model.
* The request has web search with JSON output, and the target is a Claude model.
* The request has web search with function tools or JSON output, and the target is a Gemini 2.x or earlier model.
* The request has code execution with function tools or `tool_choice`, and the target is a Gemini model.
* The request has code execution with JSON output, and the target is a Gemini 2.x or earlier model.
* The request points to state the provider stores, such as `previous_response_id`, `conversation`, `prompt`, or `background: true` in the Responses API.
  Send the full conversation instead.
* The request asks for more than one answer, such as `n` or `candidateCount` greater than 1.
* The request uses the legacy Chat Completions `functions` or `function_call` fields.
  Use `tools` and `tool_choice` instead.
* The last message is an assistant message that the model should continue.
* The request asks for JSON output with no schema, or with a schema `description`, and the target is Messages.
* The request has a Gemini `responseSchema`.
  Send the same schema as JSON Schema in `responseJsonSchema` to reach other models.
* The request has a Converse `guardrailConfig`, `outputConfig`, `promptVariables`, or `cachePoint`.
* A [Firewall](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/firewall) policy applies to the request, because Firewall can't check a translated response yet.

If every model in the request is skipped, the gateway returns [`ERR_NGROK_27228`](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/error-codes#err_ngrok_27228) with the reason for each model.
To fix it, remove the field the message names, or pick a model that serves your SDK's format.

# Use Virtual Models
Source: https://ngrok.com/docs/ai-gateway/guides/virtual-models

Give an ordered list of models one name, so you can change the models your apps use from the gateway without changing their code.

A virtual model is a name you choose, such as `chat-default`, that stands for an ordered list of models.
Your apps send that name as `model`, and you control which models it stands for from the AI Gateway.
To move to a new model or provider, edit the list, and the next request uses it.
You don't change, redeploy, or restart your apps.

When a request sends the name, the gateway tries the models in order until one succeeds.
This also gives failover to clients that can't send a [`models` fallback list](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/configure-fallback-models), such as a proxy that can't rewrite request bodies, or an agent that lets you set only one model name.

## What you'll need

* An ngrok.ai account with an [access key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys).
* Access to the models you want to list, either with [credits](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/pay-with-credits) or with [your own provider keys](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/attaching-provider-keys).
* An [AI Gateway API key](/docs/ai-gateway/concepts/access-keys#credentials-overview), if you want to use the API instead of the dashboard.

## 1. Create a virtual model

### Via the dashboard

1. Open [**Virtual Models**](https://app.ngrok.ai/virtual-models) in app.ngrok.ai and click **Create virtual model**.
2. Enter a **Name**, such as `chat-default`, and an optional **Description**.
3. Under **Models**, click **Add model** and pick the model to try first.
   Choose **Any provider** to let any provider that serves the model handle it, or choose a provider to pin the model to that provider.
4. Add each fallback model in the order you want the gateway to try them.
   To change the order, open a model's menu and move it up or down.
5. Click **Create virtual model**.

### Via the AI Gateway API

Send the name and the models to the [Virtual Models API](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/virtual-models/create):

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
curl -X POST https://api.ngrok.ai/virtual-models \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "chat-default",
    "models": [
      "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6",
      "openai:gpt-5.1",
      "google/gemini-3.6-flash"
    ],
    "description": "Default chat model for the support app"
  }'
```

The response is the new virtual model:

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "id": "aigvm_2xyzABC123",
  "uri": "/virtual-models/aigvm_2xyzABC123",
  "name": "chat-default",
  "models": [
    "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6",
    "openai:gpt-5.1",
    "google/gemini-3.6-flash"
  ],
  "description": "Default chat model for the support app",
  "createdAt": "2026-10-29T17:00:00Z",
  "updatedAt": "2026-10-29T17:00:00Z",
  "createdBy": { "id": "aigak_2abcDEF456", "uri": "/users/aigak_2abcDEF456" },
  "lastUpdatedBy": { "id": "aigak_2abcDEF456", "uri": "/users/aigak_2abcDEF456" },
  "warnings": []
}
```

## 2. Send a request with the virtual model

Use the name anywhere you'd put a model.
Nothing else in the request changes.

```python Python highlight={9} theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1",
    api_key="ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx",  # Your access key
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="chat-default",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}],
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)
```

```bash curl theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
curl -i https://gateway.ngrok.ai/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ng-xxxxx-g1-xxxxx" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "chat-default",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
  }'
```

The gateway tries `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6` first.
If that attempt fails with a rate limit, an auth error, a server error, or a timeout, it tries `openai:gpt-5.1`, then `google/gemini-3.6-flash`.

The gateway matches the name without regard to case, so `chat-default` and `Chat-Default` are the same virtual model.

Virtual models work on every endpoint that takes a model name: Chat Completions, Responses, Messages, Gemini `generateContent` and Interactions, Decisions, and System One.
On Gemini `generateContent`, put the name in the path, such as `/v1beta/models/chat-default:generateContent`.

## 3. See which model answered

Read the `Ngrok-AIG-Model` [response header](/docs/ai-gateway/how-it-works#response-headers).
It names the model that served the request, not the virtual model name:

```http theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
HTTP/2 200
ngrok-aig-request-id: rq_2abcDEF456
ngrok-aig-attempts: 2
ngrok-aig-model: gpt-5.1
```

Here the first model failed and the second model in `chat-default` answered.

To see each attempt, pass the request ID to [`GET /usage/requests/{requestId}`](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/usage/request-attempts).
Each attempt that came from a virtual model has a `virtualModel` field with its name.
See [Why a request failed over](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/why-a-request-failed-over).

## How to write the models in a virtual model

Each model in a virtual model uses the same format you'd send as `model` in a request:

| Entry | What the gateway does |
| - | - |
| `gpt-5.1` or `openai/gpt-5.1` | Tries the model on every provider that serves it, starting with the model author's own provider |
| `openai:gpt-5.1` | Tries the model on the `openai` provider only |
| `my-ollama:llama3.2` | Tries a [model you run yourself](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/use-a-model-you-run-yourself) on your custom provider |
| `ngrok/auto` | Lets ngrok.ai pick a model for each request. See [Automatic model selection](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/automatic-model-selection) |

A virtual model has these rules:

* It has 1 to 10 models.
  10 is the most attempts the gateway makes for one request.
* Each model must exist for your account when you save the virtual model: a catalog model, one of your custom models, or `provider:model` for a built-in or custom provider.
  The gateway matches provider IDs exactly, so use the lowercase **Provider ID** from the [model catalog](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/model-catalog).
* A model can't be in the list more than once.
  For example, `gpt-5.1` and `openai/gpt-5.1` are the same model.
* A model can't be another virtual model.
* If you use `ngrok/auto`, you can't add other models to the list.

The gateway doesn't check your access keys when you save a virtual model, because keys and their configurations can change later.
It checks them on each request instead.
See [Access keys apply to each model](#access-keys-apply-to-each-model).

## Name a virtual model

Names have these rules:

* 1 to 64 characters.
* Letters, numbers, `.`, `_`, and `-` only.
  Names can't contain `/` or `:`, because the gateway reads those as part of a model ID.
* Unique in your account, without regard to case.
* Different from every model your account can call, such as a short model ID like `gpt-4o` or one of your custom models.
  This keeps the name from hiding a real model.

Descriptions are optional and can be up to 255 characters.

Each account can have up to 100 virtual models.

## Combine a virtual model with a fallback list

A virtual model works with a request's `models` array.
The gateway replaces the virtual model with its models, in place, then tries the full list in order:

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "model": "chat-default",
  "models": ["deepseek:deepseek-v4-flash"],
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
}
```

The gateway tries the three models in `chat-default`, then `deepseek:deepseek-v4-flash`.

A virtual model can also be an entry in `models`.
If you list the same virtual model more than once, the gateway adds its models each time.
The gateway still makes at most 10 attempts per request, so models past that limit don't run.

### Virtual models that use ngrok/auto

A virtual model whose only model is `ngrok/auto` works the same as sending `ngrok/auto` in that position.
The [rules for combining `ngrok/auto` with fallback models](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/automatic-model-selection#combining-with-fallback-models) still apply:

* On Chat Completions, Responses, and Messages, if the request lists other models too, the gateway ignores `ngrok/auto` and uses the other models.
* On the Gemini endpoints, the request fails with `ERR_NGROK_27228`.
  The message names your virtual model: `Invalid request: virtual model "chat-auto" resolves to ngrok/auto, which cannot be combined with other models`.

## Failover works the same way

A virtual model doesn't change [what triggers failover](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/error-handling#what-triggers-failover).
The gateway moves to the next model after a rate limit, an auth error, a server error, a timeout, or a network failure.

Any other 4xx response, such as an invalid request, stops the request right away.
A virtual model doesn't route around a request that no model can serve.

## Access keys apply to each model

A virtual model never gives an access key access to a model the key can't use directly.
The gateway checks each model in the virtual model against the key's [access key configuration](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/access-key-configurations):

* If the key can't use a model, the gateway skips it and tries the next one.
  The `Ngrok-AIG-Rejected-Models` response header names the model it skipped, not the virtual model.
* If the key can't use any model in the list, the request fails with the error for the first model, the same as for a `models` list.
* Routing rules match the provider and model of each attempt, not the virtual model name.

You can't add a virtual model name to an access key configuration's allowed models.
To let a key use a virtual model, allow the models in it.
See [Restrict providers and models](/docs/ai-gateway/guides/restrict-providers-and-models#virtual-models).

## Change a virtual model

To change a virtual model, edit it on the [**Virtual Models**](https://app.ngrok.ai/virtual-models) page, or send a [`PATCH` request](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/virtual-models/update):

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
curl -X PATCH https://api.ngrok.ai/virtual-models/aigvm_2xyzABC123 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "models": ["openai:gpt-5.1", "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6"]
  }'
```

A new `models` value replaces the whole list.
Fields you leave out keep their current values.

New requests use the change with no change to your clients.
Requests that are already running finish with the old list.

If you rename a virtual model, clients that send the old name get an unknown model error.

## Delete a virtual model

Delete a virtual model from its menu on the **Virtual Models** page, or send a [`DELETE` request](/docs/ai-gateway/api-reference/virtual-models/delete).

After you delete it, the gateway treats the name like any other model name.
Clients that still send it get [`ERR_NGROK_27224`](/docs/ai-gateway/reference/error-codes#err_ngrok_27224) for an unknown model.

## Warnings

A virtual model can stop working the way you expect when something changes after you save it.
The **Virtual Models** page shows a warning on the virtual model, and the API returns it in the `warnings` field:

| Code | What changed | What the gateway does |
| - | - | - |
| `nameHidesModel` | A model with the same name as the virtual model now exists, for example a new catalog model. | Requests for the name still use the virtual model. To call the other model, rename the virtual model or name that model by its full ID. |
| `targetUnresolved` | A model in the list no longer exists, for example because you deleted a custom provider or the catalog removed the model. The warning's `target` names the model. | Requests skip that model, so you have one fewer fallback. Replace or remove the model. |

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
"warnings": [
  {
    "code": "targetUnresolved",
    "message": "'my-ollama:llama3.2' isn't a valid model anymore. Requests skip it.",
    "target": "my-ollama:llama3.2"
  }
]
```

A warning never blocks requests.

## List virtual models with /v1/models

Some SDKs, agents, and chat frontends check a model name against `GET /v1/models` before they send a request.
The gateway lists your virtual models there, after the other models, with `owned_by` set to `virtual-model`:

```json theme={"theme":{"light":"css-variables","dark":"css-variables"}}
{
  "id": "chat-default",
  "name": "chat-default",
  "slug": "chat-default",
  "object": "model",
  "owned_by": "virtual-model",
  "created": 1793293200,
  "description": "Default chat model for the support app",
  "architecture": {
    "input_modalities": [],
    "modality": "",
    "output_modalities": []
  },
  "providers": []
}
```

The list includes a virtual model only when the access key can use at least one of its models.
A new or renamed virtual model can take a few seconds to show up.
